Console

The read-mostly observability UI at /console - the complete list of what it can change, how sign-in works, the three experience levels, and what each page shows.

The console is the owner's window onto a system whose actual clients are agents. It is html/template plus vanilla JS plus SSE, served by internal/console from the same binary as everything else - no node, no npm, no React, no build step. It is not how Seamless is driven; it is how you watch it.

What the console can change

The console is read-mostly. That is a design claim, so here is the whole list - every write it is capable of, taken from the POST routes in internal/console/console.go. There are no others. A few of those routes write nothing, and their rows say so.

Action Route Effect
Archive a memory POST /console/memories/{id}/archive Routes through lifecycle.Archive: the memory is stamped invalid and leaves every index, its file stays on disk with a tombstone. Returns to the Memories list next= names, its filters kept; any other next returns to the plain list.
Force-release a task claim POST /console/tasks/{id}/release The owner override, Release claim on a task in progress, which asks in the page first: takes the task's claim from whoever holds it, live or lapsed, and tells the holder, or reopens a task marked in progress with no claim at all, so any agent may claim it. A task no longer in progress has nothing to release: the page says so (a JSON caller gets 409). Not reachable from the agent MCP tools.
Mark a task done, drop it, or reopen it POST /console/tasks/{id}/status Mark done, Drop (which asks in the page first) or Reopen on a task: to=done, dropped or open, through the update tasks_update status= makes, so a closed task unblocks the tasks that depend on it, and the last step of a plan closed as done settles the plan as an agent's close does. Records task.transition with by: console. Refused, naming the holder, while a live claim holds the task: release the claim first. Reopen is for a done or dropped task (one in progress reopens through Release claim); a move to the status the task has writes nothing.
Mark a gate as handled POST /console/tasks/{id}/gate/clear Mark as handled on a task whose own gate is open, with an optional one-line note=: clears the gate as tasks_update gate_clear does, recording the owner as who cleared it and the note. A step's gate clears, and the step goes ahead once nothing else blocks it; a gate closes as done, which unblocks the tasks waiting on it. Records task.transition with gate: cleared and by: console. Refused while a live claim holds the task, from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Force-release a repo lock POST /console/locks/{id}/release Repo locks: ends the hold a lock carries, live or lapsed, whoever holds it; the lock stays declared. What seam lock release --force sends. Refused when nobody holds it (409), from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Approve a lock declaration POST /console/locks/{id}/approve Makes a restricted account's waiting declaration an active lock, which agents may then hold. Refused for a lock already active (409), from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Discard a lock declaration POST /console/locks/{id}/discard Deletes a restricted account's waiting declaration with its repository identities, so the repository may be declared again. An active lock is refused (409): no route removes one. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Approve a captured plan POST /console/plans/{slug}/approve The escape hatch for a Claude Code approval whose PostToolUse never fired: flips the cc-plan note to plan-status:approved and creates the tracking task, exactly as the hook would have. Only applies to a CC capture.
Star / unstar an entity POST /console/favorites/{kind}/{id} Toggles the same starred flag the favorite_set MCP tool sets: a starred memory pins into briefings and gets a post-fusion recall boost. For memories and notes the star lives in frontmatter; it never bumps updated.
Ask the gardener for proposals POST /console/gardener/request Interprets a natural-language maintenance request into pending proposals. It never mutates a memory.
Plan a project split POST /console/gardener/split Interprets a split request into a plan batch of pending proposals (one split setup plus one reproject per memory). Also never mutates a memory.
Apply one proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/apply Carries out that proposal's effect.
Dismiss a proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/dismiss Drops it without acting. The pattern is raised again if new evidence for it arrives after the decision.
Hide a proposal forever POST /console/gardener/{id}/hide Drops it without acting and blocks the pattern permanently - no recurrence re-raises it. Listed under Hidden forever.
Unhide a pattern POST /console/gardener/{id}/unhide Lifts a forever block. The proposal stays resolved; the gardener may propose the pattern again the next time it recurs.
Retarget a reproject proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/retarget Rewrites a pending reproject's destination project before it is applied. Reproject proposals only.
Apply a whole plan batch POST /console/gardener/plan/{slug}/apply Applies every pending proposal in a plan, split setup first so the child projects exist before the memories move. Best-effort: it applies what it can, reports how many landed, and leaves the rest pending.
Dismiss a whole rail group POST /console/gardener/group/dismiss Dismisses every pending proposal in one rail section or split plan, one at a time, so each keeps its own event and stays individually undoable. Only Dismiss is offered in bulk.
Undo a decision POST /console/gardener/{id}/undo Returns a resolved proposal to the queue from Recently decided or the decision history, inverting whatever its apply did, for the kinds whose apply can be inverted.
Run a gardener pass now POST /console/gardener/run Runs the background proposal passes now instead of at the next pass, in the background. They only ever propose. Refused while a pass runs, and while gardener.enabled is false.
Release a held write POST /console/held/{id}/release Write screening: lands a held agent write exactly as the agent sent it, and marks the memory owner-confirmed. Refused when its target changed after it was held.
Discard a held write POST /console/held/{id}/discard Lands nothing and erases the held text; the row stays as the record.
Clear a session's outside-text mark POST /console/held/sessions/{id}/clear The only way the mark comes off: the session's changes to binding rules land without a hold again.
Turn lockdown on or off POST /console/held/lockdown on=1 or on=0. Your switch only: a lockdown the configured lockdown file holds stays on until that file goes.
Re-run the review POST /console/held/review Screens every memory and note again and marks the clean ones safe as they read now; your own marks on unchanged items stand.
Mark a flagged item safe POST /console/held/corpus/safe path= the item's file. Safe as it reads now; a memory is also stamped owner-confirmed.
Accept a file changed outside Seamless POST /console/held/corpus/accept path= the file. Records it as it stands, lifts its quarantine, and stamps a memory owner-confirmed.
Set a project's isolation POST /console/projects/{slug}/isolation Changes how far a project's knowledge travels. A tightening that would cut existing context first renders a confirmation step; nothing is written until it is confirmed.
Begin a lock change POST /console/lock/{project}/begin Only under peer_auth, and only from a signed-in browser. action=lock or remove. Refuses first a change that could not apply - a force-locked project, a lock already on, no console lock to remove, a project that is not confidential or sealed, no passkey enrolled - then returns a WebAuthn challenge naming this ceremony, the project and the direction. Writes nothing. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 ceremonies wait at once for one project and direction, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the oldest of its project and direction, and one past 32 the oldest of the project and direction holding the most. A displaced ceremony's finish says it expired.
Lock a project, or remove its lock POST /console/lock/{project}/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that ceremony, then stores the lock or removes it. Turning a lock on ends, in the same transaction, the project's agent leases, read grants and console unlocks, so every agent and browser asks again. It removes only a lock the console set: one peer_auth.force_locked holds stays. Seamless then restarts to apply the change. A finish for a ceremony that began and then failed records access.console_lock_failed under the ceremony's own project and direction, with why: the finish named another project or direction, the passkey's answer did not verify, the passkey is not enrolled, its counter did not increase, another use of it was recorded first, or the project changed since. A finish naming no waiting ceremony records nothing.
Begin a passkey unlock POST /console/unlock/{project}/begin Only for a project peer_auth locks, and only from the signed-in browser that proves its unlock key. Records a waiting console unlock bound to this browser's cookie and key, sets the seamless_unlock cookie when the browser holds no live unlock yet, and returns the passkey challenge. Refused while no passkey is enrolled; the terminal path still works. Opens nothing yet. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 passkey unlocks wait at once for one project, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the project's oldest, and one past 32 the oldest of the project holding the most. Terminal unlocks are counted apart.
Unlock a project in this browser POST /console/unlock/{project}/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that waiting unlock, from the browser that began it, and makes it live: this browser reads the project for three hours, or less when peer_auth.max_lease is shorter. It is never a lease: no agent reads the project through it.
Begin a terminal unlock POST /console/unlock/{project}/terminal Approve from a terminal: the passkey begin's gates, without needing a passkey. Records a waiting unlock bound to this browser and returns a pairing code with the seamlessd console-open --unlock command that approves it, run as the daemon's account within ten minutes. The code only names that unlock, so it is not a secret. Opens nothing until the command runs. Capped as the passkey begin is, apart from it: at most 4 wait for one project, and 32 in all.
Ask for access POST /console/access/request The agent's ask, not your decision: seam access request, run from the agent's own shell, files an access request for a locked project or, with access requests on, what the agent's conversation and a confidential or sealed project no lock covers call for: a grant, or a move into the project. With write=true it asks for a read-and-write grant or a move, a locked project's included, whose approval opens the lock too. It writes a waiting request, with the agent's reason of at most 200 characters, and opens nothing. An agent that already holds the access is answered with it.
Approve an access request POST /console/access/{id}/approve Your decision: writes the agent's lease on a locked project, or a grant, for duration= (until the session ends, 1 hour or 4 hours), and only while the request's facts still match digest=, the digest of the facts you were shown. A grant is read-only unless access=read-write on a request that offers the choice. A move request is approved for good: it ends the conversation's session and opens its continuation in the project, and duration= bounds only a locked project's lock. Under peer_auth it takes a proof: a passkey assertion from the request's page, or a Touch ID signature from Seamless Approve (proof=touchid), accepted on the peer_auth socket only and never for a move. In the advisory tier - access requests without peer_auth - a decision with no passkey is the bearer key's, which is what seam approve sends. A paired device's approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof is refused, peer_auth on or off: the bearer key's decision is never a device's.
Deny an access request POST /console/access/{id}/deny Closes a waiting request with no lease, grant or move; the project stays closed to that agent, and a move's agent stays where it works. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay: deny on the console, or with seam approve in your own terminal on the server.
Revoke an agent's lease POST /console/access/leases/{id}/revoke Revoke under Agent leases on /console/access: ends that lease before its expiry and records an access.revoked event. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Revoke a read grant POST /console/access/grants/{id}/revoke Revoke under Read grants: ends a live grant, read-only or read and write, before its expiry. Its holder stays write-confined, since a revoke does not unread what it read. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Lock a console unlock again POST /console/access/unlocks/{id}/end Lock again on /console/access, or Lock it again on the unlock page: ends any browser's live console unlock, by id. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Begin a passkey enrollment POST /console/approvers/passkey/begin Only under peer_auth: name= the passkey (1 to 64 characters on one line). Returns the WebAuthn creation options, excluding every passkey already enrolled. Holds the enrollment in memory and stores nothing. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, since a passkey is created in a browser. A begin never waits for room: at most 16 enrollments wait at once for their browser, and 16 more whose passkey exists and waits for its code, so a begin past 16 displaces the oldest still waiting for its browser, and never one waiting for its code. A displaced enrollment's next step says it expired.
Create the passkey POST /console/approvers/passkey/finish Verifies the browser's new passkey and returns its key's fingerprint with the seamlessd approvers enroll-code command that mints its code. Still stores nothing: the passkey waits for that code. Past 16 waiting for their code, it displaces the oldest of them. Refused from a paired device.
Enroll the passkey POST /console/approvers/passkey/confirm code= the one-time code that command minted for this key. Stores the passkey and uses up the code in one transaction. A code that is mistyped, expired, used or minted for another key leaves the passkey waiting, so it can be typed again. Refused from a paired device.
Enroll a Touch ID key POST /console/approvers/touchid/enroll Seamless Approve's call, from the app seam touchid enroll opens, accepted on the peer_auth socket only - never with the TCP key or the console cookie. Stores the Mac's new Touch ID key, proven by an enrollment code minted for that key and the key's signature over it. An earlier Touch ID key of the same Mac that signs its own retirement is retired in the same step. No console route removes any other credential: that is seamlessd approvers remove.
Begin a passkey sign-in POST /console/signin/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey, and only from a browser that proves its key (the login page sets it up). Returns the WebAuthn challenge, bound to that key and to a ticket that works once. Writes nothing. A 404 while the key signs browsers in.
Sign in with a passkey POST /console/signin/finish Verifies the assertion for that challenge, from the browser that began it, records the passkey's use, and sets a fresh random sign-in cookie that counts only with this browser's key, for 7 days. A cookie the browser held before ends with it.
Begin adding a passkey POST /console/passkeys/add/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey: the public Add a passkey page asks for the new passkey's name=. Returns the WebAuthn creation options. Writes nothing.
Add a passkey, waiting POST /console/passkeys/add/finish Verifies the device's new passkey and stores it as waiting, with a short code, for 10 minutes. It adds nothing: seamlessd approvers approve --code, on the server, adds exactly that passkey. It never waits for room: at most 4 wait at once from one address (an IPv6 address counts by its /64, and every loopback address is one), and 32 from every address but loopback, whose 4 are its own. One past its address's 4 displaces that address's oldest, and one past the 32 the oldest of the address holding the most; a displaced passkey's code names nothing, and its page says to add it again. So someone looping on the page from one computer crowds out only their own, and no number of other hosts reaches a passkey added on the server itself. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address.
Begin a terminal sign-in POST /console/signin/terminal/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey, and only from a browser that proves its key: Show a code on the login page. Sets a fresh random sign-in cookie bound to that key and stores it waiting, with a short code, for 10 minutes, with the address the request came from and its User-Agent (printable ASCII with each run of spaces as one, at most 256 characters), which the answer also carries for the page to show beside the code. It signs nothing in: seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code, on the server (as the daemon's account under peer_auth, at a terminal), shows those and when it began, asks, and on a yes signs in exactly the browser that showed that code, for 7 days. It never waits for room: at most 4 wait at once from one address (an IPv6 address counts by its /64, and every loopback address is one), and 32 from every address but loopback, whose 4 are its own. A begin past its address's 4 displaces that address's oldest code, and one past the 32 the oldest of the address holding the most; a displaced code approves nothing, and its page says to show a new one. So someone looping on Show a code from one computer crowds out only their own, and no number of other hosts reaches a code a browser on the server itself showed. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address. A 404 while the key signs browsers in.
Get a pairing code POST /console/devices/code Only on a server that serves other computers (TLS, a bind beyond loopback, or a server_url naming another host). Mints a one-time pairing code, valid for 10 minutes and for one computer, and shows it once, in this answer, with the client one-liners, which carry the server certificate's fingerprint when it serves TLS; only its hash is stored. Without peer_auth the code is the approval; under peer_auth the pairing it starts waits for a passkey. At most 16 codes wait at once. Refused (409, pairing needs TLS here) where the server's address is plain http to another host. Refused (409, server_url names a user) where it names a user. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device, peer_auth on or off.
Begin a device approval POST /console/devices/{id}/approve/begin Only under peer_auth, from a signed-in browser, for a pairing that waits, or for a relay that waits for its approval in place: active, paired with its one-time code alone, and mapped in peer_auth.relays. Returns the WebAuthn challenge, bound to that device's id, kind, name, fingerprint and key (and, in place, to its status and that purpose), and a ticket. Writes nothing.
Approve a device POST /console/devices/{id}/approve/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that ticket over the device as it stands, records the passkey's use, and pairs the device: a relay's certificate is accepted from its next request, and a key device collects its own key, once, on its next status. A relay waiting in place is approved where it stands, the same device id and certificate, in one compare-and-set that refuses a relay revoked meanwhile; its requests are judged from the next one on, and an access.device_paired event marked in_place records it.
Revoke a device, or deny a pairing POST /console/devices/{id}/revoke Revokes a paired device: its credential is refused from its next request, and the requests it is making end. A pairing that waits is denied instead. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device, peer_auth on or off.
Save briefing settings POST /console/settings/briefing Writes the briefing knobs as a runtime override row in the DB. It never writes the config file.
Reset briefing settings POST /console/settings/briefing/reset Clears the override row, reverting to the file/env configuration.
Preview a briefing POST /console/settings/briefing/preview A read, not a write: it POSTs only to carry the Briefing form's unsaved values, which it checks with the save's own validation, and answers with the briefing a new session in the chosen project would start with. Writes no settings row and records no event. A locked project is not previewed.
Force utility ranking for a scope POST /console/settings/utility Sets or clears the owner's per-scope force: on and off win over the gardener's readiness latch, auto defers to it again.
Switch embeddings off or back on POST /console/settings/embeddings/mode Stores or clears the embedder off switch. It is read at serve start, so the change applies from the next restart - the page says so.
Re-embed everything POST /console/settings/embeddings/reembed Starts a background pass that re-embeds every memory and note with the active model. It changes vectors, never content.
Choose the console level POST /console/settings/level Stores the experience level as a row that wins over file and env. Presentation only: nothing an agent receives changes.
Reset the console level POST /console/settings/level/reset Clears that row, back to the file/env level.
Dismiss the welcome card POST /console/settings/level/welcome Records that the Home welcome card was seen, without choosing a level. With the card's write-screening box ticked, it also turns that feature on, as a level choice with the box ticked does.
Save optional features POST /console/settings/features Writes the feature switches as a stored override row in the DB. It changes what is exposed - console screens and the matching agent tools - and deletes nothing.
Reset optional features POST /console/settings/features/reset Clears the override row, reverting to the file/env configuration - which, unless you set the keys there, means every optional feature is off again. Still deletes nothing.
Turn update checks on or off POST /console/settings/updates Stores the console's update.check override (check=on or off). It cannot turn checks on while the config file or environment says update.check: false - that is final, and the form says so. Off is your decision alone: refused (403) from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, whatever checks are now; on is open to them. Installs nothing.
Reset update checks POST /console/settings/updates/reset Clears that override - both switches - handing them back to the config file (or, without one, the build's default). A build that is not a published release does not check by default, so there a reset that drops this console's check=on turns checks off, and automatic updates with them: it is refused like turning them off, unless the file or environment locks checks off already. It is refused even where the file's update.check: true would keep them on, since the console cannot see the file's update block under its own override. Every other reset, and every reset on a release build, is open to any caller.
Check for updates now POST /console/settings/updates/check Asks GitHub's release list once, right away - refused while checks are off or within a minute of the last check. Reads; installs nothing.
Turn automatic updates on or off POST /console/settings/updates/auto Stores the console's update.auto override (auto=on or off), keeping its update.check. It cannot turn automatic updates on while the config file or environment says update.auto: false, or locks update.check: false (nothing installs without checks). With checks merely off, the choice is kept and applies once they are back on. Off is your decision alone, refused as turning checks off is; on is open to any caller. Only an install that updates itself acts on it: the installer's, or a peer_auth system daemon's.
Update now POST /console/settings/updates/apply Installs the newest release at once, after a confirm: it skips the soak, the wait for idle agents, skipped releases and the backoff, and lifts a hold, whether automatic updates are on, off or paused. Refused while checks are off, on an install that does not update itself, while an update is under way, within a minute of a failed release check, when nothing newer is known, or when the release carries no signed checksums bundle. The daemon restarts to finish.
Resume automatic updates POST /console/settings/updates/resume Lifts the pause automatic updates put on themselves after rollbacks, and the hold a deliberate downgrade set. Changes no setting; skipped releases stay skipped, and a running backoff runs out.
Save the backup schedule and folder POST /console/settings/backups Stores the console's backup: override: only the values that differ from the settings in force. A new folder is created and tested with a write first. Applies from the next backup.
Reset the backup settings POST /console/settings/backups/reset Clears that override, handing the schedule and the folder back to the config file (or, without one, the build's default).
Back up now POST /console/settings/backups/now Writes a backup at once, marked Made by you: never skipped, never deleted automatically. With run=retry (the failing card's Try again) it runs the schedule's backup instead, which is skipped when nothing changed and prunes after itself. Refused while a backup runs or a restore is being prepared.
Delete a backup POST /console/settings/backups/delete ref= a backup from the list, never a path. Removes the file from its folder, after a confirm.
Begin a restore's passkey ceremony POST /console/settings/backups/restore/begin Only while peer_auth locks a project, and only from a signed-in browser. Returns a WebAuthn challenge bound to the backup file's SHA-256, which the server reads from the file itself, and to the mode. Writes nothing. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 ceremonies wait at once for one backup and mode, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the oldest for its backup and mode, and one past 32 the oldest of the backup and mode holding the most. A displaced ceremony's finish says it expired.
Restore a backup POST /console/settings/backups/restore ref= and mode=replace or merge. Verifies the backup and prepares the restore while Seamless serves, then restarts to finish it. A replace saves today's data as a backup first. Refused while a backup, another restore or an update is under way. Under the passkey gate it also needs the ceremony's id and response, and the file's digest must still match.
Cancel a staged restore POST /console/settings/backups/restore/cancel Drops a restore that is waiting for its restart. Nothing changes.
Dismiss a restore's result POST /console/settings/backups/restore/dismiss Hides the last restore's result card. Changes no data.
Save a project family POST /console/settings/families/save Creates a family or replaces one family's name and member set - the same project_families setting seamlessd family manages. Members come from a closed picker of registered projects, so a typo cannot create an inert member.
Delete a project family POST /console/settings/families/delete Removes the whole family. Its projects lose the sibling-findings channel; nothing else about them changes.
Sign in / sign out POST /console/login, POST /console/logout Sets or clears the console cookie. Touches no data.

Your decisions come through a paired device only as your own hands. On a server that serves other computers, a request that comes with a paired device's credential - a relay's certificate or a device key - is refused (403) on every write that is yours to make: a pairing code and a device's revocation, Held's release, discard, session marks, lockdown and corpus marks, the optional features, turning update checks or automatic updates off (and a reset that would turn checks off), every Backups route, bringing a project's fence down, a deny, a revoke, Lock again, a passkey's enrollment, and an approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof. That holds with peer_auth on or off, with one exception: under peer_auth, a request through a relay you map whose process chain the server judges your own hands there - every process named, none an agent, the chain whole, and your uid there the one both the mapping and the relay's pairing name (the rule) - makes them, and each one it makes records an access.relay_decision event (item: the relay's device; payload: its name, your uid there, the route and the chain's programs by name). Its approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof still goes to the approve core, which refuses it: a chain is no proof. A key device, a relay to a server without peer_auth, and any other chain carry their agents, never your hands, and the refusal says why: make these decisions in the console of the server you sign in to, in a terminal on the server itself, or in a terminal of your own behind a relay you map. The reads stay open to a device, and so do the writes an agent may make: seam on a client computer reads the console's JSON through its relay, and the Touch ID helper there approves through it with its own signature.

Read the shape of that list. There is no "create memory", no "edit note", no "delete memory", no "add task", no "start session". The direct writes to knowledge state are archive a memory, approve a captured plan, the star flag, and - with write screening on - releasing a held write, which lands exactly what an agent wrote, never text of the console's own; the rest either manage gardener proposals - which are themselves proposals, reviewed before they do anything - or free a task claim, or set a configuration knob (briefing overrides, feature switches, project families, the update switches, the backup schedule and folder) that shapes future briefings, what is exposed, or how the install runs, without touching any memory's content. Back up now and Delete a backup make and remove copies of the data, never the data itself. The console level is presentation state of the same kind: it changes what this console shows you and nothing else. The access, lock, unlock and approver rows exist only with peer_auth or access requests on (both optional, and off by default; every one of those routes answers 404 otherwise), and they are your decisions about who may reach a project, not writes to knowledge: they record requests, leases, grants, moves (a move ends the conversation's session and opens its continuation in the project it moved into), console unlocks, locks and approver credentials, and never a memory's or a note's content. The one an agent calls, Ask for access, only files a request for you to decide. Update now and Resume automatic updates act on the install rather than on knowledge: the first starts the same backed-up update seamlessd update runs, the second lets automatic updates run again. A restore is the one write that changes knowledge wholesale, and it puts back what a backup of this install held, never text of the console's own: the data from before is saved as a backup first, so a restore is itself undone by restoring.

This is deliberate, and it is the same principle as the gardener's propose-only contract. The store is written by agents doing work, with provenance attached. A console that could quietly edit a memory would produce knowledge that came from nowhere, attributable to no session, explaining nothing.

Every write action redirects back with a flash message (?notice= for success, ?error= for failure) rather than rendering a result page in place, so a reload never repeats the action. With script, a success notice surfaces as a toast and both parameters are stripped from the address bar, so a later live refresh never replays a message about an action that already happened; an error also stays on the page as a banner.

Signing in

There is one credential in the whole system: the static bearer key (mcp.api_key). It guards /api/mcp, the hook endpoints, and the console alike.

Two ways to present it:

  • A browser trades the key for a cookie at /console/login. The cookie value is a SHA-256 hash of the key, not the key - so the raw credential never sits in the browser's cookie jar. It is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and scoped to /console.
  • The seam CLI sends the key as a bearer token on the Authorization header, and asks for JSON.

Unauthenticated browsers are redirected to the login page with a ?next= that is validated against an open-redirect (an off-site or absolute candidate becomes /console/). Unauthenticated JSON callers get a 401.

Public routes are the login page, the static assets (console.css, interactions.js, search.js, favicon.svg and the rest under /console/static/) and the service worker at /console/sw.js. Everything else requires the key.

A browser sends its cookies to every port of the same host, so a program that can open your browser on another local port receives the console cookie too. Today that adds nothing to what reading the key gives such a program. A console unlock of a locked project is worth more, and so is a passkey sign-in, so neither is just a cookie: each also needs a key the browser keeps for the console's own address, and a service worker signs each console request with that key. The service worker runs in a browser that has started an unlock, and under passkey sign-in in every signed-in browser. Before an unlock or a sign-in the page asks the daemon for the worker again, and when an upgrade brought a new one, it waits while the new worker takes over, so the old one never signs for the new daemon. The worker and its key script (/console/static/browserkey.js) are served no-cache, so the browser checks with the daemon each time it loads them. The other static files are linked by version (After an upgrade).

Sign in with a passkey

Set console.sign_in: passkey in the daemon's config (off by default; file only) and restart it, and a browser signs in with a passkey you added, in any browser, the server's included. No browser needs the key: the login page no longer takes it, and a cookie derived from it signs nothing in. The seam CLI keeps sending the key.

  • Signing in. The login page sets up the browser's key and service worker, then asks for your passkey: this device's, one your password manager syncs here, or your phone's through the browser's QR prompt. The daemon answers with a random cookie and keeps only a hash of it and the browser's key together, so the cookie read on another port opens nothing. A sign-in lasts 7 days in that browser, or until you sign out from the sidebar (which also drops its console unlocks), or until the passkey that made it is removed. A restore signs every browser out.
  • A page drawn without the proof (a hard reload skips the worker) lands on the login page, which sets the worker up and asks for the page again. A browser that cannot run a service worker (some private windows) cannot sign in.
  • Adding a passkey for a new device. On the server, seamlessd approvers add prints the Add a passkey address (/console/passkeys/add on the passkey origin). It is not a secret: anyone who reaches the console can open it, and nothing is added until you approve. Open it on the device and create the passkey; the page shows a short code and the key's fingerprint. Run seamlessd approvers approve --code 7KQ2-M9XD on the server (as the daemon's account under peer_auth; the page shows the exact command). It shows the same name and key and asks before it adds, so it runs only at a terminal (over ssh, ssh -t), and no flag skips the question. Approve only a code your own device shows.
  • No passkey at hand. Under Sign in from a terminal on the server, the login page's Show a code begins a terminal sign-in: the browser gets a cookie bound to its key and shows a code with the command that approves it, /usr/bin/sudo -k -u _seamless /usr/bin/env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code 7KQ2-M9XD under peer_auth (seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code 7KQ2-M9XD without it). Approved, that browser is signed in for 7 days, as with a passkey, and the page goes on by itself. The command first shows the browser the code names (when it began, its address and User-Agent) and asks; say yes only to a code your own browser shows you now. The code signs in no other browser, so reading it off your screen gives nothing away. It is the way back in when every passkey is lost: add a new one from the Add a passkey page.
  • Synced passkeys. A passkey synced through iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or another password manager is one passkey: add it once, and every device it syncs to signs in, with nothing more to add. A device without it can use your phone's passkey through the browser's QR prompt.
  • The server's name. A passkey works only for the name it was made for. One made for another site, or for localhost on another install, does not work here. With localhost passkeys only a browser on the server itself can make or use one. Renaming the server, or turning TLS off, strands every passkey made for the old name (doctor names them).

make console

make console          # open in the default browser, already signed in
make console-chrome   # same, but force Google Chrome

This builds, then runs seamlessd console-open, which renders a one-shot self-submitting login page to a 0600 temp file and opens it. The page POSTs the key to /console/login, which sets the cookie and 303s into the console - so you land on an authenticated page with nothing to paste. It refuses to run if mcp.api_key is empty or the server is not answering /healthz. Under passkey sign-in, console-open opens the sign-in page instead and writes no page and no key.

make console-chrome exists for agents: they drive Chrome, so this hands the auth cookie to the browser they can actually see. (--browser is macOS-only.)

Getting around

The sidebar groups the screens by the job they serve rather than by table:

Group Screens
Live Overview, Now, Interactions
Knowledge Memories, Notes, Retrieval, Gardener, Held (only while write screening is on, or restricted accounts are configured)
Work Diary (only while that optional feature is on), Projects, Plans, Tasks, Sessions, Locks (only while that optional feature is on)
Research Labs, Trials (only while that optional feature is on)
Server System, Privacy, Devices (only on a server that serves other computers)
Access Access requests, Approvers (only while peer_auth locks a project)

That is the full list, at the Advanced level; a lower level shows a subset, in the same order and under the same names. Settings closes the list. Above the groups, a Search or jump to field opens the command palette. The sidebar collapses to an icon rail (the header button, or [) and remembers that per browser; under 720px it becomes a drawer behind the menu button, with every section's label and count.

Every screen title carries an (i) button that says, in one line, what the screen is for.

The command palette

Cmd/Ctrl+K, the sidebar's search field, or / on a screen with no filter of its own opens the palette. With nothing typed it offers Recent (the entities you last opened in this browser), Jump to (every section the sidebar offers, with its shortcut, plus Search, Context, and each Settings section the level shows), and Actions (switch theme, collapse the sidebar, the shortcut sheet, change the experience level). Typing matches sections and actions instantly; from two characters on it also searches memories, notes, tasks, plans, trials, projects, and sessions through the same route as Search, showing the groups the level offers. Each group shows up to five, starred matches first and marked starred; a group with more shows its count as 5+ and ends with More in Search, which opens Search narrowed to that kind. An exact name of a superseded or archived memory finds it here too, with its status.

Keyboard

Keys Does
Cmd/Ctrl+K Search or jump to a section
/ Focus this screen's filter; open the palette where there is none
g then a key Go to a section: o Overview, n Now, i Interactions, m Memories, e Notes, r Retrieval, g Gardener, h Held, d Diary, w Projects, p Plans, t Tasks, s Sessions, b Locks, l Labs, x Trials, y System, v Privacy, c Devices, a Access requests, k Approvers, , Settings
j / k Next / previous item in a library rail
[ Collapse or expand the sidebar
? The shortcut sheet
Esc Close the palette, a menu, the sheet, or the drawer

The g map is read from the sidebar itself, so a section switched off in Settings - or one the level leaves out of the sidebar - takes its shortcut with it, and brings it back when it returns.

Moving between screens keeps the sidebar in place and settles the new content in (cross-document view transitions, where the browser supports them), and hovering a console link prefetches its page. Neither runs any code of the destination page early; both degrade to a plain navigation.

Ambient signals

The console shows activity without asking to be read. The line along the sidebar's edge - the Seam - carries each event from the live stream as a spark that travels to the section it belongs to and lights that section's icon: cyan for context reaching an agent, green for knowledge written, coral for something wrong, indigo for everything else. Each event also rings the daemon's dot in the sidebar and the page's live dots once, and the sky behind the pages brightens with the recent event rate and settles when the fleet is idle; the dot dims while the live stream is down. Headline numbers count up when a page opens; agents working right now carry a slow orbit of light on the Now screen.

All of it is decoration over data the page already states: nothing here changes a number, and prefers-reduced-motion stills every part of it (the Seam sends no sparks, numbers render at their value). Between events the sky and the sidebar hold still, so a console left open on the Overview draws nothing while the fleet is idle.

After an upgrade

Every page links its stylesheet and scripts by their version, a digest of the file this build serves (/console/static/console.css?v=...). The browser keeps each one until a build changes it, so the first page load after an upgrade uses the new stylesheet and scripts, and loads after that fetch none of them again. A static file asked for without its version, such as the worker's import of browserkey.js, is checked with the daemon on each use.

A tab left open across an upgrade keeps the stylesheet and scripts it loaded first while its views update in place. When the daemon now serves different ones, the page says so once, in the corner: "Seamless was updated. Reload this page to use the new version." The console never reloads the page itself; Reload does, when you choose.

Choose how much you see

The console has three experience levels. They change what the console shows you and nothing else: your agents get the same briefing, the same MCP tools, the same hooks, the same recall, and the same gardener at every level. The level is presentation, stored for this installation's owner rather than per browser, so your phone and your laptop agree.

Basic is the essentials, for someone who installed Seamless because they use Claude Code or Codex and wants to know it works: what the agents remember (Memories, Notes), what they did (Sessions), cleanup suggestions to accept or decline (Gardener), and a Home that opens on a health strip - which agent clients are working here, whether semantic recall is on, when the last briefing went out, and the version (which says when a newer release is out) - plus the Updates and Backups settings.

Standard adds following the work: Now, Projects, Plans, and Tasks (and Labs and Trials when that feature is on), the Overview's window, vitals, and workspaces, the Briefing and Workspaces settings, and the finer controls on the screens Basic already had.

Advanced is every screen and every knob: Interactions (the tool-call transport), Retrieval (the analytics), Context, the Knowledge engine settings, and raw event payloads.

A fresh installation starts at Basic, and Home carries a one-time welcome card offering all three - pick one, or dismiss it; either way it does not come back, on any device. Beside the levels the card offers one optional feature as an unchecked box, Also turn on write screening: it rides with whichever button you press, and unticked it changes nothing at any level. It is a feature, not part of a level, because it changes what your agents receive (see Held); once the card is gone, Settings > Features is the way in. The sidebar's account row names the level you are on and links to Settings > Experience, where the three levels sit side by side with the list of what each one shows. The palette's Change experience level action goes there too.

Hidden, not locked. A level removes screens from the sidebar, the palette, and the shortcut map; it never locks them. A link to a screen above your level - from these docs, an agent's finding, a briefing, a bookmark - still opens it, under a note saying it is not in your sidebar, with a button to switch. JSON callers (?format=json, and so the seam CLI, seam doctor included) get the same answer at every level.

Upgrading keeps every screen. An installation that already recorded sessions before levels existed is set to Advanced by a one-time upgrade step, so nothing you were using disappears; Settings > Experience says the level was set by the upgrade, and the welcome card appears once to announce the choice.

Levels and optional features compose: a screen shows when its feature is on and the level includes it. Features change what exists - for the console and for agents alike; the level only changes how much of it you see. The level can also come from the config file or environment (console.level, SEAMLESS_CONSOLE_LEVEL) - a choice made in the console wins until you reset it there. See Configuration.

Three ways to render a page

Every route answers in the shape the caller asked for:

  • HTML by default - the full page, layout and all.
  • JSON when the caller sets ?format=json or an Accept header that wants JSON and not HTML. This is how seam reads the console's data.
  • An HTML fragment for entity details when the caller passes ?peek=1 - the detail pane loads it without a page navigation - or ?reader=1, the richer reader fragment the library screens (memories, notes, tasks, plans, labs, trials) swap in place.

The event page composes its full page from the same detail-body block its peek fragment renders, so the two cannot drift. Session and project deliberately do not: their fragments are compact summaries of much richer bespoke pages. Memory, note, task, plan, lab, and trial detail URLs render their library screen with that entity open in the reader.

Strictly-validated query params (?sort, ?scope, ?tab, ?w) return a 400 naming the bad param and listing the valid values, rather than silently falling back to a default - so an agent driving the console by URL sees the fix.

GET /console/events is the SSE stream: every recorded event as one JSON data: frame, with a ping every 25 seconds. A retrieval.injected frame also lists the memories it surfaced as itemIds (capped at 48), which is what lets a page point at exactly what reached an agent. ?feed=interactions opts into the richer transport-level rows the Interactions screen consumes.

Overview

/console/

The landing page and the health check. It carries:

  • Counts - active memories (broken down by kind), notes, sessions, and tasks by status.
  • Retrieval health over a selectable window (?w=24h|7d|30d|all): injection volume, a trend chart, the reach rate (distinct active memories that actually surfaced, over all active memories), sessions reached, and the most-injected memories.
  • Coverage - the share of in-window sessions that retained anything, with a per-channel breakdown (findings, memories, notes, trials) and a windowed trend. The channels overlap, so the shares need not sum to 100%.
  • Projects at a glance - the top projects by recent activity, drawn from the same batched query the Projects board uses, so a row here reconciles with a row there exactly.
  • Agent-reported mishaps - while any report exists, the attention strip's first card counts the mishaps agents reported at session_end (the newest six) and names the latest one's type, age and project. With one report it opens that report's event page; with more, the Mishaps screen.
  • Going stale - the attention strip's knowledge card counts the active memories with no update, injection, or read in gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default, the gardener's own staleness horizon), exactly the rows Retrieval's quiet-knowledge list shows, and states the horizon. Changing the setting moves the card, the list and their labels together.
  • Knowledge sky - a star chart of every active memory, with no cap. Each project scope (global included) owns a wedge sized by its share of memories, largest first. Distance from the centre is when the memory last surfaced to an agent: the core holds the last 24 hours, rings mark 7 days and the staleness horizon, gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default; the same fresh and stale lines the memory reader's "since surfaced" chip uses), and the rim belt holds memories that have never surfaced. Colour is kind; size is demand (the query-gated utility score, so a big star is one agents pull, not one the briefing merely shows). Hollow stars have never surfaced, a ring marks a starred memory, spikes mark one written today, and today's stars twinkle as the chart appears. Beside the chart, a readout states the same picture as text: each ring's count, the going-stale count (memories with no update, injection, or read within the staleness horizon: always the attention card's count and the rows Retrieval's quiet-knowledge list shows), and every scope with its ring mix as a bar. Point at a star for its name and description (the pointer snaps to the nearest star); click it for a card with its facts and a link to open it; double-click to open it directly. Type in Find a memory to light only the matches (name, description, tag, scope, or kind) and list them, with the arrow keys and Enter to step through; click a ring, the going- stale line, a scope, or a kind chip to filter the same way, and point at one to preview it. When an injection or a read lands on the live stream, each memory it names sends a beam into the core, and the refresh that follows glides the star to its new ring; a newly written memory appears with a flare. A star keeps its place while its scope and ring are unchanged, and the rings and wedges resize in steps rather than with every memory, so a refresh moves only what changed, and search, filters, and the selection survive it. The refresh downloads only what changed, too: the stars that changed, arrived, or left since the chart the page holds, and nothing of the sky when nothing in it did. It is HTML only - the JSON answer carries no sky.
  • Recent activity - the last twelve events, each linking to its detail page.

The four judged vitals at the top (memory reach, knowledge continuity, context injections, sessions reached) are drill-down links carrying the selected window: reach, injections, and sessions reached land on the Retrieval screen whose hero and delivery funnel are the same numbers over the same report, and continuity lands on the Sessions list filtered to ?retained=no - the sessions that kept nothing. An empty-state card stays linked, because the destination explains why there is nothing.

Live sessions are counted TTL-aware (active and heartbeated within the idle threshold), so the headline matches the Sessions screen rather than the raw active count that an idle session inflates until the reaper runs.

Since you were last here

When you come back to the Overview after at least five minutes away, a line above everything else answers the check-in question -- what changed while I was gone? -- with linked counts: memories written, sessions started, tasks closed, notes written, gardener proposals raised, and mishaps reported since you last looked ("Quiet since you were last here 3h ago" when nothing was recorded).

"Last looked" is a per-browser stamp, set whenever a console tab is hidden or left; the counts come from GET /console/since?t=<unix ms>, which answers JSON only and refuses a missing, malformed, future, or older-than-90-days t with a 400 rather than substituting a window.

Now

/console/now

The exploded live view: what every agent is doing right now, across every project and plan at once. Where the project workspace is task-centric, Now is agent-centric - the unit is the live session, and everything it holds rides its card. The sidebar entry's badge is the live agent count, and the page refreshes on every event kind (tool calls included - here they are the signal, not noise), morphing in place like every other screen.

Top to bottom:

  • The titlebar - live agent count and the fleet-wide pulse: an events-per- five-minutes sparkline over the last hour, all kinds, deliberately unfiltered by scope.
  • A scope strip - one chip per project with a live agent (?scope=<slug>; the empty project scope filters as global). Filtering narrows every zone except the pulse.
  • On duty - one card per live session: harness+model pill, project, last heartbeat (cards are toned hot/warm/quiet by heartbeat age), session wall clock, cumulative tokens, a star toggle, every claim it holds with a live lease countdown, and a short trail of what it just produced. A live agent holding nothing says so: "no claim held - roaming".
  • Loose ends - in_progress tasks no live agent is carrying: a lapsed lease, a claimless start (tasks_update status=in_progress without a claim), or a holder that went quiet mid-lease. A lapsed claim offers release claim with no confirmation - the lease is already dead, so there is no live holder to interrupt, only a stale claim to clear.
  • Plans in motion - a horizontally scrolling rail of every incomplete plan across every project, done/in-flight progress bars and ready counts, cards dimmed once a plan has rested for 24h. Each links to its project's Plans & tasks tab.
  • Up next - the cross-project ready queue: claimable this instant, plan steps included, each naming what closing it would unblock.
  • The wire - the freshest business events, scope-filtered.

Everything links onward - sessions, tasks, plans, projects, events - and the lease countdowns tick client-side between refreshes. With the gamification feature on, the page also carries the day tape, the personal-records rail, the hot-streak pulse, and celebration moments; off (the default), none of that renders.

Interactions

/console/interactions

The clean live feed of what agents are actually doing: MCP tool calls, hook injections, recall-miss prompts, session lifecycle, and the plan-mode capture stream. A fresh page starts empty and listens from that moment forward; merely visiting never restores old rows.

History is explicit and additive. Choose a recent window and select Add when earlier context is useful; live rows stay in place, and Load older events paginates only inside that chosen window. Filters operate over the rows already in memory, by event category and session lane. Pausing buffers new arrivals rather than discarding them.

Each compact row expands just enough to expose its request/result or injected text. Selecting the inspector keeps that context beside the stream and links to the full event page. A recall via the MCP tool records both a retrieval.injected and a tool.call; the injected twin is dropped here because the tool call carries the same content plus its arguments. Session lifecycle twins are kept on purpose, as feed markers.

Search

/console/search

One query across every entity the console can link to. Memories and notes come through the same fused FTS + semantic retrieval that recall uses, with snippets; tasks, plans, trials, projects, and sessions have no FTS mirror and match by LIKE.

Counts are honest. Each kind shows up to 20 results and is fetched one further, so a kind with more says so: its count reads 20+ and its Show more opens up to 200 of that kind (?more=tasks, comma-separated for several). Show more is part of the address, so it survives the live refresh and the Type, Updated, Starred, Archived, and Sort controls; a new query starts with it closed. A kind still cut at 200 says how many it shows and asks for a narrower search. The header's total carries the same + when any kind was cut. Memories and notes are counted apart, so many matching memories never squeeze the notes out.

Each kind wears one color wherever Search names it: its count in the results header is the legend for its rows, and the Type filter, the palette's group heads and an empty page's type chip carry the same color as a dot. Archived and superseded memories wear a quieter take of the memory color.

Starred only (?fav=1) runs inside each query, before the cut, so a starred match ranked past the first 20 still appears. Without it, a kind's starred matches take its first slots, then the best of the rest.

Superseded and archived memories, which every other search leaves out, have their own lookup here. An exact memory name or ID always finds one, under Archived & superseded, badged superseded (with a link to the memory that replaced it) or archived. Include archived (?archived=1, offered while memories are in scope) finds them by text as well. A locked project's retired memories stay out, like the rest of its content.

A one-character query says to type at least two characters. A query that finds nothing lists each restriction in force - the type, the Updated window, Starred only - as a chip that removes it, with Clear all filters when there are two or more; when archived or superseded memories match where nothing live does, it says how many and offers Include archived.

Stable references get their own lookup lane. An exact memory name or note slug ranks ahead of token-overlap matches and is shown beside the result's display title. A full memory, note, task, session, or trial ULID works case-insensitively; an 8-character-or-longer ULID prefix finds every match of those kinds without letting a short prefix such as 01 flood the page. Identifier matches keep the canonical ID-based detail link and are labeled separately from keyword and semantic matches.

The command palette (⌘K, available on every page) fetches this same route with ?format=json&fast=1, which drops the semantic leg - a query per keystroke must never cost a remote embedding round-trip.

The semantic leg is nearest-neighbor: there is always a "nearest" memory, however far, so a semantic-only hit must clear search.semantic_floor (cosine similarity, default 0.3) to appear - without the floor any query, including nonsense, would fill the page to its limit. A hit the keyword leg also matched is exempt. Every hit the semantic leg found shows its similarity as a percentage, so you can see where relevance falls off; keyword-only hits show a highlighted snippet instead. Agent-facing recall applies no floor - an agent can judge a weak hit for itself.

Coverage is deliberately partial in one place: events are excluded because the telemetry stream has its own Interactions surface and would flood results.

Diary

/console/diary, /console/diary?day=YYYY-MM-DD

Only while the Diary optional feature is on. Then it shows at every level, as the first row of the sidebar's Work group, and g then d opens it. It is a page for each day of work: what was worked on, which agents did it, and what it took in agent time and model tokens, with the meaningful work in the spotlight and short question-and-answer sessions folded away. A day runs from midnight to midnight in the daemon's time zone, so a daylight-saving day has 23 or 25 hours. The page is composed from what Seamless already records (the usage ledger, the event log, the sessions, tasks, memories, notes, trials and commit records), by stated rules and no model.

/console/diary is today; ?day= is another day, and &m=YYYY-MM shows another month in the rail beside it. A day or m that does not parse is a 400 that names the format.

What a day shows

The date block. The weekday, the date, and the day's character as a stamp whose tooltip states its rule. The character is the first of these the day meets:

Character Rule
Quiet No session, task or item recorded
Shipped A plan shipped: its last open step closed as done
Closing day 5 or more tasks closed as done
Planning day A plan drafted (captured, presented or approved) or 6 or more tasks created, and fewer than 2 closed
Deep work 2h or more of agent time, 60% or more of it in one project
Busy day 3h or more of agent time, 12 or more sessions beyond the short ones, or work in 4 or more projects
Light day Work recorded, under every threshold of a fuller day

Under it, the headline: "Mostly X: ..." when one thing took at least half the day's agent time (or was the only thing worked on), "Led by X: ..." otherwise, saying what it did ("1 step closed and the plan shipped (5 of 5)"). Its second sentence counts the day's sessions, where they were, and how many things they worked on. Then Sessions started this day (N), and under peer_auth a line naming the locked projects this browser has not unlocked, whose work the page leaves out.

Four tiles. Agent time, model tokens, tasks closed (closed as done and still done at the day's end) and kept (the distinct memories, notes and trials written, new or updated). Each states the usual day and draws a trend line over the last active days, then this one; past days also carry the change against the usual day, in percent and never judged good or bad. The usual day is the median of the active days before this one (a day with a session, a task closed or an item kept): up to the 14 most recent within 90 days, and no comparison at all with fewer than 3. Today's tiles show no change, since part of a day against a whole one would read as a fall every morning, and its agent time and tokens say "so far". Each tile jumps to the part of the entry that lists what it counts.

Day rhythm. One column per hour, agent time stacked by agent, the busiest hour's figure on its column. A column's full height stands for at least an hour of agent time, so a light day looks light.

What was worked on. The day is written in threads. A plan thread is one plan in one project: the steps that moved that day and the sessions that moved them or captured, presented or approved the plan. A project thread is one project's tasks outside any plan that moved, and its sessions whose work named no plan or task; sessions in no project make a thread named after their working directory's last folder. The spotlight's threads are cards: the plan's progress before and after the day ("12 → 14 of 14 steps closed"), each task that moved with its status before and after, each session with its agent, what it was about, its agent time and tokens, then the hours it was worked in, the thread's figures, what its sessions kept and the commits it recorded, and a Why this is here disclosure listing the facts that scored. The other threads are one line each under Also that day, and the short sessions one collapsed row, N short sessions.

What a session was about is the first of these that exists: the first line of the findings its agent wrote, its first prompt of the day, the first line of the findings the hooks harvested from its transcript, or "Session in project". The sentence links to the session.

The usage panel. Agents: a ring of model tokens by agent (one client and one model, named as its pill reads), the day's total in the center and a legend row per agent with its share and figure; a day with one agent draws its legend line and no ring. Token mix: output, fresh input, cache write and cache read, as one bar. Projects: bars by agent time, or by model tokens on a day with none. Then Tasks closed, Kept (a superseded or archived memory is marked), and Moments: plans shipped, commits recorded (with what recorded them), flags set, and mishaps the agents reported. Show as table lists every figure the charts draw.

The rail. The month as a heat grid shaded by agent time, then its days, newest first: each with a bar of its agent time against the month's busiest day, the figure, a dot for each of its top projects, and its sessions and character in the tooltip. A run of quiet days is one thin row, and a day from before the usage ledger shows its agent time as "—", not 0m.

The spotlight

A thread scores its outcomes and its effort, each fact capped so that no single one carries a thread alone:

Fact Points At most
The plan shipped: its last open step closed as done 10 10
Each task or step closed as done 3 12
Each task or step created or claimed 1 3
Each memory, note or trial its sessions wrote 1 4
Each commit its tasks or sessions recorded 1 4
Each session that ended with findings its agent wrote 1 2
Agent time 1 for every 10 minutes 12
Output tokens 1 for every 80,000 6

A thread needs 4 points to be a card, and at most six are, most points first. A thread holding a flagged session is always a card, whatever it scored, and counts toward the six. Why this is here lists each fact with the points it scored.

A session's part of a day is short when it has no outcome, under 10 minutes of agent time and under 30,000 output tokens, and is not flagged. An outcome is something the record keeps: a task moved, a plan captured, presented or approved, a memory, note or trial written, a mishap reported, a commit recorded, or an end that day with findings its agent wrote (a summary the hooks harvested does not count). A short session is never a card or part of a thread: it is one line in the folded row, and the character's session and project counts leave it out.

Agent time and model tokens

Agent time is a count of minutes in which an agent sent at least one model message, counted for each session, model and thread (the agent's own turns, and the subagents it launched apart), and added up. Agents working in parallel, and a session beside its subagents, make more agent time than the clock passed.

Model tokens are the four kinds the token mix shows, added: output, fresh input, cache writes and cache reads. They include cache reads, so they are not a billing figure, and the Diary shows no cost.

A day's totals come from the usage ledger with each session counted once; they are never the sum of the cards. Three words mark where a figure is less than whole:

  • Unreported - a session with no token record at all. It is named in a note under the tiles, counted as "(N unreported)" on the tokens tile and on its thread's card, and never counted as zero. A Claude Code session reports at its end, and while the Diary is on its prompts keep it current (mid-session usage); a Codex session reports at each turn's Stop.
  • Approximate - a session from before the usage ledger, which has token totals and no ledger rows. Its whole total counts on the day it ended and on no other ("counted on Nov 12"), with no hour, thread or agent time: the tokens tile says approximate, a note under the tiles says why, and agent time reads "not recorded before the usage ledger". seam usage backfill replaces it with real rows while the session's Claude Code transcript is still on its computer (the command).
  • Shared - a session that worked on more than one thing (two plans, or a plan and loose tasks) is in each thread, and counts in full in each: a card's figures say how many of its sessions are shared, and the cards never add up to the day.

Links

Every link is built from an id resolved, as the page renders, through what this browser may read. An item that no longer exists is plain text titled "No longer exists": the Diary never offers a link that answers 404. A link into an optional feature exists only while that feature is on. A link to an entity opens it beside the day as a peek; a modified click opens the full page.

On the Diary Opens
A day in the rail, a cell of the month grid, the previous or next day, Today That day, in place. A day still to come is never a link; the month arrows keep the day and change the month the rail shows.
A task The task's page.
A session's line, its flag badge The session's page, where its flag and any kept transcript are.
A memory The memory's page; a superseded or archived memory keeps its page, and the Kept list marks it.
A note The note's page.
A trial The trial's page, only while Research is on. With Research off, trials are not on the page at all.
A mishap Its event's page.
A plan: a card's title, a shipped moment The plan's page when it has one in that project; otherwise that project's Plans & tasks tab, as a page; a plan in the global scope with no page is text.
A project chip, a project bar The project's page; the global scope and a working directory are text.
A commit The page of the task or session that recorded it (a commit has no page of its own), with a button to copy its full id.
Sessions started this day (N) The Sessions screen's list for that day, which lists the sessions created on it: hence "started", and N is that list's count. The day's own session count, in the headline, also holds sessions started earlier that worked on it.
A tile The part of this entry that lists what it counts.

The agents legend, the rhythm's columns and the token mix are not links: no page lists "this agent's sessions that day", so they answer on hover only. The other way in is the Sessions screen: a day view there carries Open in Diary while the Diary is on.

Moving around

Keys Does
← / → The previous / next day (today has no next)
t Today
Arrows, Home, End, Esc in a chart Walk its marks, jump to the first or last, rest
Arrows, Enter in the month grid Move a day or a week, open the day

The day keys stand down while you type, while a dialog is open, inside a chart or a peek, and after g, which belongs to the section shortcuts.

How the charts answer. Every mark answers on hover or a tap: a ring segment, an hour of the day rhythm, a project bar, a part of the token mix, a day of the month, a stretch of a card's presence strip. The readout gives its figures and the rest of the chart goes quiet. From the keyboard each chart is one tab stop. Days and project names are real links, so a modified click opens a new tab and the grid works without scripts. Colors name agents only: an agent keeps one color for the whole month, and agents past the month's five busiest share a neutral Other, whose readout names them. A card's presence strip lights whole hours, so its readout gives a stretch of hours, not agent minutes.

Peeks. A peek opens beside the day on a window 1380px wide or more, and under it below that, and the item you clicked stays where it was. Back closes it, and a #peek= link opens the day with it open. Changing the day happens in place and keeps the browser's history.

Today is live. It refreshes in place from the console's live stream, at most every 15 seconds, and an open peek stays open. A past day does not refresh.

On a phone the entry comes first and the month after it, and the tiles go two by two.

With Research off, trials appear nowhere: the day's kept counts, a thread's kept list and its points, the headline and the character are composed without them. The rail and the usual day still count trials among the items kept (counts, never an item).

Empty days

  • A quiet day: "A quiet day.", with no tiles or charts: no session, task or item was recorded.
  • The first run: a day with nothing recorded on it, in its month or in the 90 days before it says "This is the Diary's first page." and draws no stamp.
  • A day still to come: "This day has not begun." and "Still to come.", with Back to today.
  • A day of only short sessions: "Only short sessions: they are folded below."
  • A day from before the usage ledger: totals marked approximate, and agent time not recorded.

The JSON answer

?format=json answers with the day model, the same at every level: the day and its bounds (day, start, end, hours, today), headline, character (word and rule), facts (the tiles' and the character's counts), usage (by agent, project and hour, with the token mix, unreported and approximate), spotlight and also (the threads, each with its score and reasons), short, kept, moments, sessionsStarted and projects; then month (the rail's month, its days and its agents) and usual (the usual day). Every item the day names carries its kind, id, title, resolved and href, the link the page shows, empty when the item no longer resolves or its feature is off. A day still to come answers "future": true with every list empty.

Projects

/console/projects

Locks. Under peer_auth, a confidential or sealed project's Isolation card offers Lock this project, which opens /console/lock/<project>. Locking it, and removing a lock set here, each need a passkey already enrolled on the Approvers page; without one the card links there. Seamless restarts to apply the change. A project listed under peer_auth.force_locked shows as Force locked and cannot be changed here. A locked project's isolation cannot be set to open.

The board: one row per project, with live sessions, total sessions, open and blocked tasks, memory count, inherited memories, reach rate, and last activity (the later of its last session update and its last task change). It has three views (?group=activity|family|flat):

  • Activity, the default: Active (a live agent, or a session or task touched in the last 30 days), then Quiet, then Retired. Quiet and Retired are folded. A filter (?q=) that matches a project inside one opens it, and Quiet stands open when no project is Active.
  • Family: each shared-briefing family, a parent with its children under it, then Standalone, then Retired by split, folded.
  • Flat: every project in one list.

?sort=recent|coverage|name|favorites orders the rows inside each band. In the Activity view, Recent puts starred projects first, then those with a live agent, then the most recent.

The global ("") scope is not a project, so no view lists it. It is one line under the summary tiles, "Shared context: N memories, N notes, reach N%", linking to Context.

Under peer_auth, a locked project this browser has not unlocked is a row in the same bands, sorted with the others, with a lock badge: its name, its counts, its last activity (the latest session start or end in it, never a title) and Unlock, which opens /console/unlock/<project>. Nothing else about it is read. The JSON model also lists these tallies as locked.

The board remembers the view and sort you pick, in this browser only (its local storage). A link that names neither, such as the sidebar's, shows the remembered pair, drawn in place without a reload; a URL that names a view or a sort wins. A fresh browser starts on Activity, sorted by Recent.

Selecting a project opens the project workspace - a seven-tab page over that project alone:

Tab Shows
Overview The project's metrics, memory kinds, injection trend, recent events.
Plans & tasks Per-plan step timelines with each step's status words, claiming session, lease countdown, and blocking dependency; plus the ready queue. Each row copies its task's whole id, and each plan's head copies plan:<slug>.
Sessions The project's sessions, with the tasks each currently holds.
Memories The project's memories with a lineage cell - provenance session, or a supersession pointer - plus the memories it inherits from a parent that a strict per-slug count excludes.
Notes The project's notes.
Interactions The project-scoped slice of the feed.
Context The effective SessionStart flow into and out of the project: global and parent memory pools, sibling-family channels, and split lineage.

Came from. With access requests on, an item written by an agent that held a confidential or sealed project's content carries a provenance stamp ("may contain content from example-finance (grant R-7F3K)"). On a project with such items, the Memories, Notes and Plans & tasks tabs show the stamp on each row and a Came from bar: one chip per project the stamps name, with how many items of that tab's kind name it. Choosing one (?from=<project>) narrows the three tabs to those items, and Plans & tasks then lists the tasks themselves, any status. A locked project this browser has not unlocked is named only; the items listed are this project's own. A project with no stamped item shows no bar.

A retired project still renders, with its banner - kept for provenance. Only an unknown slug is a 404.

Sessions

/console/sessions, /console/sessions/{id}, /console/sessions/{id}/transcript

The list separates active (live: active and heartbeated within the idle TTL) from idle (active but gone quiet past it, awaiting the reaper) from completed and expired. Filterable by status, searchable, windowed, and filterable by retention (?retained=yes|no): whether the session left a durable artifact behind - non-empty findings, or a written memory, note, or recorded trial, the same covered-ness test the coverage numbers apply. The Overview's continuity vital links straight to ?retained=no, so its click answers "which sessions dropped knowledge".

The list defaults to the last 24 hours (?w=24h|7d|30d|all; any other value is refused). When that leaves most sessions out, the list ends by saying so ("3 of 212 sessions were active in the last 24h") and offers the wider windows in place, so a quiet day never reads as an empty system. A row names its host only when the session ran on a different machine from the console's, and its source only when it was not a normal startup.

A day view (?day=YYYY-MM-DD, what a click on the momentum calendar opens) lists the sessions started on that day, whatever the window. While the Diary is on, its heading carries Open in Diary, that day's page.

A session's page is the workspace: its findings (rendered), its full event timeline as interaction rows, per-session counts (tool calls, memory reads and writes, items injected, and read-after-inject), the tasks it currently claims with their lease countdowns, and the memories it produced.

A flagged session carries a badge with its verdict (good, bad or notable) and its reason on the list, the peek and its page. Its page adds a card: when it was flagged, the transcript file the agent client wrote, and what became of the copy, with Download JSONL while a copy is kept (/console/sessions/{id}/transcript, the owner's alone: never a restricted account, a relay's caller or a paired device). Once any session is flagged, the list offers a Flag filter (?verdict=flagged|good|bad|notable). With no window chosen it lists the flagged sessions of all time, as seam sessions --flagged does: a flag changes no session's last update, so the 24-hour default would hide a session flagged after its day. A window chosen under Updated applies to the filter as to every other, and stays chosen while the other filters change; until then the page's links carry none.

The conversation
