With access requests on, a conversation can span sessions: a move into a fenced project continues it as a child session there. Every session of a conversation that moved, asked for or holds a grant, or wrote a stamped item shows one Conversation card (also in the page's JSON as conversation):

  • Home chain: the session it started in and each move's child, oldest first, with the move's request, who decided it and when.
  • Reach: every project it reached - its homes, projects session_start bound it to, read-only and read-and-write grants, leases, and requests still waiting, denied or expired - each with its request (R-...) and who decided it: a passkey or Touch ID key by name, the terminal (seamlessd approve), the bearer key (seam approve or the console, advisory), the agent's approval dialog (advisory), or a Deny on this console.
  • Written: what its sessions wrote, by project, each with its provenance stamp.

A locked project this browser has not unlocked shows its name, the request that reached it and an Unlock link back to the page, and nothing from inside. A conversation that never moved, asked for nothing and wrote nothing stamped shows no card.

Mishaps

/console/mishaps

Every mishap agents reported at session_end, newest first, for a recurrence review: which kinds keep happening, and which memories fail to prevent them. It has no sidebar entry; the Overview's mishap card and the palette's Jump to open it.

  • Type chips - All, then each type with its count - shell-trap, wrong-target, live-state, ignored-warning, fabricated, other - and untyped: reports that named no type, among them every report written before types existed. The counts cover the project and window in view whatever type is selected; point at a chip for what its type means.
  • Reports - each with its type (or untyped), its text with the type prefix taken off, its project (click it to keep only that scope's reports), the session that reported it with its agent, and the memories it named. Click a row to open its event beside the list.
  • Memories named - every memory the reports in view named, with how many named it. A memory many reports name is one that is not preventing its mishap.

Filters: ?type= (a type, or untyped), ?project= (a slug, or global), and the window ?w=24h|7d|30d|all (all time by default) or ?days=N. A value the page cannot read is a 400 naming what it takes. ?format=json answers total, types (each with its count and meaning), shown (the reports the filters select), mishaps (each with type, text, the recorded description, project, sessionId, session and memories), memories (each with its count), and locked while peer_auth leaves locked projects out. The list holds the newest 200.

Memories

/console/memories, /console/memories/{id}

A two-pane library: a rail of memories beside a full-height reader. Under the default sort, Recent, the rail is one list, newest first, each row carrying its project and its kind, so what changed last is at the top. Group: Project turns it into a tree - global first, then projects A to Z, kinds in canonical order within each, every kind group with a one-line subtitle saying what that kind holds - and the Name sort always draws the tree. The other sorts are reach (how often a memory surfaced), utility, and starred. Inactive memories collapse into an archived-and-superseded group at the rail's end, each carrying its status and, when superseded, what replaced it.

Filters narrow the rail and combine: Kind, Project (a project, or the shared global scope), Starred, and Never surfaced - memories that have never reached an agent's context. Each menu entry and toggle counts what choosing it would show. The text box matches a substring of the name, the description, the kind, a tag, or the project's slug or name. While anything is filtered the header reads "3 of 128 active" beside a Clear link; when nothing matches, the rail says so and offers Clear and Search everything for the same text on Search.

The whole state is in the URL - ?sort=, ?group=project, ?kind=, ?project= (a slug, or global), ?fav=1, ?surfaced=never and ?q= - and it survives what you do on the page: opening another memory, changing the sort (the memory you are reading stays open), starring, and archiving (you land on the same filtered list). A value the screen cannot read is a 400 naming the values it takes.

What reaches an agent's context is surfaced here, the word the Overview and the knowledge sky use: a rail row reads "surfaced 43×" or "never surfaced", and the reader leads with how long since the memory last surfaced, or says it never has. A kind chip's tooltip is the same one-line meaning its kind group shows.

The reader renders the body uncapped (through the markdown layer, with raw HTML disabled and a sanitizer on the output), the metadata - kind, project, tags, timestamps, the session that produced it - how often it surfaced and was read, the sessions it surfaced to (the five latest, each linked, the rest behind all N), its utility score with the per-signal demand breakdown behind it, the vscode:// link straight to the file, and its supersession neighbors in both directions: what replaced it, and what it replaced. The actions here are star - the flag that pins it into briefings and boosts recall - and archive.

Opening /console/memories auto-opens the first match (in the tree, the most recently updated one); a memory's own URL opens the same screen with it selected. Clicking rail items swaps the reader in place (real URLs, browser Back works), and j / k step through the rail.

Notes

/console/notes, /console/notes/{id}

The same library shape for notes: under Recent the rail is one list, newest first, each row carrying its project; Group: Project groups it by project (global "" first), and sorting by title always does. Sortable by recency, title, or starred; filterable by Project and Starred and by a substring of the title, the description, a tag, or the project's slug or name, with the same "N of M" header, Clear, Search fallback and URL state as Memories. The reader renders the note as a document - uncapped body in a measured reading column, description, tags, word count, source URL, and the file path with an editor link. A plan:<slug> tag is a link to the plan with its status: a captured plan's own, otherwise in progress, ready or done from its steps. The tags software adds - created-by:*, plan-status:*, cc-plan and agent-cache - fold behind a +N chip.

Tasks

/console/tasks, /console/tasks/{id}

The same library shape, with the rail grouped into four buckets: ready (no unfinished blocker), in progress, blocked, and closed (done and dropped merged, newest first, capped at 25 with a count of the rest, collapsed by default). The reader carries the task's body, claim and lease state, and both dependency directions, and the owner's actions on the task, the same in the reader and in the peek (the step dossier on a project's Plans & tasks tab): Mark done and Drop on an open or in-progress task, Reopen on a closed one, Mark as handled with a note on an open gate, and Release claim on a task in progress, whoever holds it or none. Drop and Release claim ask in the page: the button turns into a second one to press. While a live claim holds the task the page names its holder and offers Release claim first: the console never closes a task over its holder's head. Each action returns to the page it came from with a line that says what it did.

Every task and plan step says where it stands in the same words, on Tasks, the project workspace and Plans:

Word Means
ready Open, with nothing unfinished before it: an agent can claim it now.
in progress Held by a live claim.
blocked Open, waiting on unfinished work before it.
waiting on who A gate, or a step an open gate holds - its own, or a gate it depends on - named by who must act (waiting on owner).
claim lapsed In progress, but its holder's lease ran out: any agent can claim it.
unclaimed Marked in progress without a claim (seam task start, or tasks_update status=in_progress): any agent can claim it.
done, dropped Closed.

A task's holder and creator are named by their session and link to its page when the console can read it. The lease reads lease live, 12m left while the claim holds and lapsed 3m ago once it runs out.

Each task row - a rail row, a plan step, a ready-queue row, a dependency - shows the last 8 characters of the task's id with a copy button beside it that copies the whole id, the form you hand an agent (run <id>). In a list the button stays quiet until you hover or focus the row; on a touch screen it is always there. A plan copies as plan:<slug>.

Hover a relative time (3d) to see the moment it names, in your browser's own time; without JavaScript the hover shows it in UTC.

Under a lock, a task blocked by a task in a locked project you haven't unlocked sits in the blocked rail, its blocker named only by project on a line of its own; the task's reader and peek list it under Depends on the same way. The project workspace's Plans & tasks tab marks such steps blocked and leaves them out of the ready queue. Opening a plan or a session that lives in a locked project takes you to that project's unlock page, which says the item is there and links back once you unlock it.

Locks

/console/locks, /console/locks/{id}

Only while the Repo locks optional feature is on; a Standard screen. Every repo lock, shown with its repository and its name (LOCK seamless main): the refs it guards, whether it is free, held or lapsed, the session that holds it with since and until (and the restricted account that session belongs to, when it is one), the lock's queue while sessions wait for it (how many, and the next one, with its account when it is a restricted account's), the repository identities that resolve to it, and the projects whose restricted accounts may hold it. A lock belongs to no project, so the page lists every one; a holder or a next waiter in a project this browser has not unlocked reads "a session this console does not show", and such a listed project is left out.

  • Waiting for your approval - the declarations restricted accounts filed: nobody can hold one until you Approve it, and Discard leaves the repository free to be declared again. The sidebar badge counts them.
  • Force release - on a held or lapsed lock: ends the hold whoever holds it. The agent that held it is not told, so release a lock only when its holder is gone or stuck.

/console/locks/{id} is the same page with that lock marked; with ?format=json, the lock alone.

Plans

/console/plans, /console/plans/{slug}

The same library shape, with the rail grouped by phase (in progress, ready, done) and scoped by the window selector in the rail's tools (24h by default). Both kinds of plan share the rail:

  • captures - Claude Code plan-mode captures (cc-plan notes), with their lifecycle status, iteration count, and cached subagent runs.
  • composed - plain plans-as-composition plans (a note tagged plan:<slug> plus its tasks), which have none of the capture-only fields.

When the window hides plans, the rail ends with how many last moved before it and the wider windows to switch to.

A capture owns its slug; composed plans fill only the rest. The reader shows the rendered plan body, the step tasks (each in its status word, with a copy button for its id), and the notes attached to the composition (supporting notes and agent caches). Approve appears here, for captures only.

Each plan also carries a model tokens rollup - the cumulative transcript tokens of every session attributed to the plan (any session that moved a step, or captured the plan) - compact in the rail (~483k tok) and qualified in the reader (~483k model tokens · 3 sessions (1 unreported)). Attribution is whole-session on purpose: tokens are only ever known per session, so a session's full burn counts toward each plan it touched, counted once however many steps it moved. Claude Code reports tokens at session end (and, while the Diary is on, as its prompts keep its usage current), so a live session stays unreported until then; a session that touched more than one plan is disclosed as shared rather than split by guesswork - which is also why plan totals must never be summed across plans.

Labs

/console/labs, /console/labs/{name}

The research-lab surface (the console twin of lab_open / trial_record / trial_query). Labs and Trials are one optional feature and ship off; while it is off both screens answer with a short "switched off" page and neither appears in the nav.

A lab is not a stored entity - it is the label its trials carry, a stable name for one line of investigation - so this screen is an aggregation over the trials table and there is nothing to write.

The same library shape: a rail of labs, most recently active first, each with its trial count and pass/fail tallies. The reader shows one lab's whole identity - outcome tallies (pass, fail, partial, inconclusive, and other for free-form or empty outcomes), the projects and sessions its trials touched, first and last activity - and its trial history, newest first, each entry linking into the Trials screen. Long histories cap at 100 with a pointer to the uncapped, filterable view.

Trials

/console/trials, /console/trials/{id}

The flat, filterable view over every recorded trial - the console twin of the trial_query MCP tool, and part of the same optional feature as Labs. The rail groups trials by lab (a group sits where its newest trial does) and filters by ?lab= and ?outcome=. Outcomes are free-form by design, so ?outcome= is an exact-match filter rather than a validated enum; the seg offers the conventional values (pass, fail, partial, inconclusive).

The reader shows one trial's full record: what changed, expected vs actual side by side (the actual pane tinted by outcome), the structured metrics trial_record captured, and its provenance - lab, project, and the recording session, each linked. Trial hits also surface in search and the command palette, and a session's page lists the trials it recorded.

Context

/console/context

The briefing topology that the plans board does not show: which knowledge pools are eligible at SessionStart, which configured edges are currently enabled by the effective briefing settings, and where project splits moved durable memory. It covers global memory, one-way parent-memory inheritance, bidirectional sibling families (findings and the opt-in memory channel), unregistered-scope warnings, and retired-project split lineage reconstructed from the memory-move event log.

?scope=all renders every known project scope, with global memory shown as the shared source pool; ?scope=project&project=<slug> focuses the same topology on one project. The legacy /console/relations route permanently redirects here and preserves its query string.

Reachable from the Projects board.

Retrieval

/console/retrieval

The circulation report: is stored knowledge actually reaching agents, and at what cost? The hero pairs the reach ring (distinct active memories that surfaced, over all active memories) with the window's volume and cost - injections, sessions reached, and estimated tokens injected. Everything follows the selectable observation window except where a panel says otherwise.

Five zones below it:

  1. Delivery path - the funnel as a flow: injections → distinct memories → sessions reached, ending in the knowledge-base coverage meter (how many active memories are still waiting to surface).
  2. Circulation pattern - the injection trend chart and the traffic-by-kind mix.
  3. Scope coverage - reach per project scope (global first), each row with its own reach rate and injection count.
  4. Knowledge pressure - the most-injected memories against quiet knowledge: active memories not updated, injected, or read within gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default), the horizon the gardener's staleness pass proposes archives by, and the label says the configured value. Unlike everything else on the page, the stale list is all-time, not windowed. Each row links to its memory and, when the gardener already holds a pending proposal for it (an archive, a merge, a move, a reclassification), to that proposal: proposal waiting. The staleness pass never proposes archiving a constraint, a stage, or a memory another memory links to, so such a row can stand without one.
  5. Loop health - push versus pull: is what briefings push also what agents pull? Demand rate is the share of briefed memories that were also pulled by a query; waste share is the share of injected tokens spent on memories with no query-gated demand, judged against a fixed trailing 30 days whatever the window. Two miss stats sit side by side and measure different paths: the recall-miss rate is ambient - prompts that matched no memory on the <seam-recall> path - while agent search misses are deliberate recall calls that found nothing; recurring ones feed the gardener's memory-wanted pass. Funnel by surface splits the read-after-inject funnel by injection surface - session-start briefings versus subagent-start child injections - each with its injections, distinct memories, and the share pulled by a query-gated read within the following 24 hours. The zone closes with the dead weight panel: memories briefings kept injecting without a single recall hit, prompt match, or read in 30 days (constraints and stages exempt as pinned-by-design) - the evidence behind the gardener's dead-weight archive proposals. Its rows link to a waiting proposal the same way.

Reachable from the Overview's retrieval-health card.

Gardener

/console/gardener

The review queue. Each pending proposal renders as a card showing exactly what it would do - the memory to archive and why (whether staleness, a dead stage, or dead weight flagged it), the pair to merge with their similarity score, the digest or consolidated memory with its body rendered, the reproject's source and destination, the rekind's from and to kinds, the split's children and shared parent, and the knowledge gap card with the queries agents kept searching for in vain - applying that one opens a task; nothing is written until someone writes the memory.

Split batches are grouped by plan and reviewed together, setup card first, with an apply-the-whole-plan action.

A status line under the head says what the background passes are doing: when the last pass ran and when the next one is due, each check a pass skips and why (dedup with no embeddings, digest with no chat model, a pass the config turns off), and any check that failed. An empty queue reads "The garden is tidy" only after a pass that ran every check; otherwise it says what did not run. Run a pass now starts the passes without waiting for the next one; it is refused while a pass runs. With gardener.enabled: false the line reads "Suggestions are off", no pass is offered, and the upkeep the same schedule carries (idle sessions reaped, old tool events pruned, retrieval stats refreshed) still runs. The line carries no counts: a pass spans every project, a locked one included.

The actions are apply, dismiss, hide forever, retarget (reproject cards only), and apply plan. Dismissing answers the evidence in front of you - the pattern comes back if it recurs; hiding answers the pattern itself. A proposal changes nothing until it is applied, by you here or by an agent with gardener_apply, and every decision records who made it. The newest ten land in Recently decided with an Undo; the decision history (/console/gardener/decisions) pages through all of them, newest first, with the outcome, who decided (you, an agent's session, the gardener settling a proposal whose memory had gone inactive, or unknown for a decision made before this was recorded), the note or task an apply produced, and Undo wherever it can be taken back. A hide is additionally listed under Hidden forever, where Unhide lifts the block without returning the proposal to the queue. Above them sits a single ask-in-words box, and it only ever produces more proposals for this same queue. A request recognized as a project split is planned as a split directly - the plan batch appears below like any other. When the split's source project cannot be matched, an inline follow-up asks you to pick the project and plans the split from there; nothing is retyped.

See The gardener for what each proposal type means.

Held

/console/held - while write screening is on, at every level (whoever turns it on must reach what it holds).

The owner's queue of agent writes kept out of the corpus. Each card says what the write would do (a constraint memory, a note, a delete, a gardener apply), which project, tool and session it came from (the project and the session link to their pages), and why it was held - each reason code with its meaning in words, the most serious first, each in its kind's color (a secret red, an injection marker orange, hidden text violet, hidden characters pink, an unlisted link indigo, an encoded blob teal, a binding-rule policy amber, a restricted account's proposal blue); the card's edge takes its most serious reason's color. Below that is the write exactly as an agent would read it: every hidden character spelled out as [U+XXXX], and secrets redacted, so the page can be reviewed and captured without the credential it holds. What each reason matched is marked in the text in that reason's color (hover a mark for its reason), and where matches overlap - an override phrase inside a hidden comment - the marks nest, so none hides another. The Review and Changed outside Seamless cards mark their findings the same way.

A held update of an existing memory or note opens on What releasing changes instead: a line diff of the write against the file as it stands now, each removed line marked - and each added line +, unchanged lines beyond three either side of a change folded into a count, with the same treatment and marks. The whole write follows, folded. A write that matches the current file line for line says so. A held new item shows its text alone.

  • Release lands it through the files layer as the agent wrote it, and the memory reads [owner-confirmed] in briefings from then on. A held supersede releases both halves together; a held delete removes the memory; a held gardener apply applies the proposal. When the target changed after the write was held, only Discard is offered: a release would silently undo that later change.
  • Discard lands nothing and erases the held text.

At the top, Lockdown says whether lockdown is on and what holds it, with the switch; a lockdown the configured lockdown file holds says so, and only that file going lifts it.

Below the queue, Changed outside Seamless lists the memory and note files the drift watch quarantined - changed or planted on disk by something other than Seamless - with their verdict codes, the sessions they were injected into before, and their text with the same treatment as a held write. Accept records one as it stands and lets agents receive it again. Review counts the review's verdicts (safe, flagged, not reviewed), lists each flagged item the same way with Mark safe, and offers Re-run review.

Sessions that read outside text lists every session an agent guard marked, with its reason and a Clear mark button - the only way a mark comes off. Recently decided keeps the last twenty releases and discards, without their text. The sidebar badge counts what is waiting.

Proposals from restricted accounts. Under peer_auth, a restricted local account's change to a constraint, convention, protocol or stage waits here too, as a proposal: its card says "Proposed by account ", and its button reads Promote instead of Release. Promoting lands it exactly as written, still labeled with the account; seam promote does the same from your terminal. While write screening is off, a daemon that lists restricted accounts still serves this screen, showing the proposals only - no lockdown, review or session marks - and the sidebar badge counts the proposals.

Elsewhere on the console, a memory, note, task, session or trial that a restricted account wrote carries a small "written by account " chip (a task whose title or body the account rewrote, "updated by account ", until you have rewritten all of its text; a status change or a claim moves neither chip), including search results, a lab's trial list and the project workspace's tabs; events and a session's activity timeline carry none. Your own items show none.

System

/console/system

Every part of Seamless on this server, drawn as one 3D base: the doors where agents and you come in (MCP, hooks, the peer_auth socket, the listener, the console, A2A), the work the daemon does (retrieval, tasks and plans, sessions, labs, approvals, write screening, updates, commit records, the metadata feed, URL capture, the gardener, lifecycle), the core that keeps knowledge on disk (the database, the file watcher, memory and note files, embeddings, the search index, the chat model, backups, the event log), and the outside services it calls (the LLM provider, GitHub releases).

  • State is the server's. Each part is running, quiet (on, with nothing in the event log for the last 15 minutes), needs attention, or off - drawn grey, with what turning it on takes. The header counts each state; click a count to light only those parts.
  • Motion is evidence. A part moves only while it works, and light runs along a trace only along the path a recorded event's data took: a memory write runs from MCP through the memory files, the watcher and the database to the search index, and on to embeddings and the provider. With nothing recorded the view is still and draws no frames.
  • Pick a part - on the deck or in the list under it - for its readout: what it does, its numbers for the last 24 hours, events per minute for the last 30, its settings, the parts it works with, and the screen that holds more. #<part> on the URL opens one directly.
  • Light on the GPU. It draws only while something changes, never while the tab is hidden or the view is scrolled away, keeps to a pixel budget on very large displays, and asks for the low-power GPU. Still (and the system's reduced-motion setting) keeps everything in place.

It is a Standard screen: Basic installs reach it by URL.

Privacy

/console/privacy

What your agents can reach on this server, what one could do if it were compromised, and where each project's knowledge may go.

  • Your setup - whether Seamless runs as your own account or as its own (peer_auth), and five protection layers: project fences, write screening, Seamless in its own account, locked projects, and a restricted agent account, each on, off, or waiting on an earlier one.
  • Who can reach what - the machine drawn as a plan: rooms are OS accounts, walls are what the operating system enforces, doors are how Seamless is reached. Switch between your account, a dedicated account and a dedicated account with restricted agents, and turn on Compromised agent to see how far one gets in each: in your own account it reads every project's files directly, sealed ones too, and takes the bearer key; in a dedicated account the data folder is out of its reach and a locked project waits for your approval.
  • Where knowledge is allowed to go - your projects around the global scope, with the flows each fence allows.
  • The four fences - open, confidential, sealed and locked, always all four, empty or not: what each promises, what kind of project belongs there, the projects in it, and how to put a project there. A locked project shows by name and counts only.
  • Find the fence for a project - three yes-or-no questions that end in a recommendation and its command.
  • What to do next - the steps that would tighten this server, in order.

It reads; it changes nothing. It is a Standard screen: Basic installs reach it by URL.

Devices

/console/devices

Only on a server that serves other computers (TLS, a bind beyond loopback, or a server_url naming another host); elsewhere the page and its routes do not exist. The computers paired with this server, and how to pair another (the guide):

  • Pair a computer - this server's address and its certificate's fingerprint, and Get a pairing code: a code shown once, valid for 10 minutes and for one computer, with the client one-liners, which carry the fingerprint for setup on the other computer to compare. The code works once, so the line left in that computer's shell history is dead after use. Without peer_auth the page says the code is the approval. Where this server's address is plain http to another host the page says pairing needs TLS, and offers no code. Where it names a user the page shows it without the user, says to take it out of server_url, and offers no code. Where it is this computer's loopback (no server_url on a wildcard bind) the page says the one-liners carry it, so another computer cannot use them, and that server_url is the fix; it still offers a code, for a client on this computer.
  • Waiting for your approval - under peer_auth only: each computer that used a code, its fingerprint and until when it waits, with Approve with a passkey and Deny. Approving needs a signed-in browser on the passkey origin and an enrolled passkey; the page says which is missing. A relay paired with its one-time code alone, while peer_auth was off, waits here too once peer_auth.relays maps it: it is refused until Approve with a passkey approves it in place, the same device and certificate, so it need not pair again, and Revoke ends it. The JSON lists it under in_place, not paired. A revoked or expired relay is not offered.
  • Paired - each relay and key device: its key's fingerprint or the start of its key, when it paired, whether your passkey or its one-time code approved it, when it was last seen, and Revoke. A relay shows the uid its pairing recorded as yours on its computer; without peer_auth one that recorded none (paired before, or by a relay of an earlier release) is warned about: re-pair it to bind the owner's uid. From 14 days before this server's certificate expires, and past it, the section names every relay paired here: a renewal means re-pairing each relay.
  • Revoked and expired - what ended, when, and from where.

It shows at every level, in the sidebar's Server group; g then c opens it.

Settings

/console/settings?s=<section>

Settings is one section at a time, each shaped by what you came to do rather than by subsystem. A sub-nav on the left (a row of chips on a phone) switches sections in place, without reloading the page. /console/settings alone opens Experience; an unknown ?s= is a 400 that names the valid sections. Which sections a level offers is in the matrix above; a section above your level still opens from a link, under the same note a hidden screen gets. Old /console/settings#... bookmarks land on the matching section.

The editable sections share two habits. A one-line note at the top says where the values come from - Following file + env, or an override in force, with Reset to file + env beside it. And a save bar appears at the bottom once a form has unsaved changes, with Save and Discard (which puts the form back exactly as the page loaded it); without JavaScript the bar is simply always there. GET /console/settings?format=json returns the whole payload whatever ?s= says, plus consoleLevel, consoleLevelOverridden, and consoleLevelSource.

Experience

/console/settings?s=experience

The three levels side by side - Basic, Standard, Advanced - the current one marked, each with a one-line pitch and a list of what it shows, generated from the same registries the sidebar and the page gates read, so the list cannot promise something the level does not do. Choosing one applies at once: the sidebar and the page update in place, and if the new level hides the screen you were on you land on Home with a note. The note at the top says whether the level was chosen in the console or set by the upgrade, and Reset to file + env hands the choice back to console.level. The same section holds the theme and a button for the shortcut sheet. The theme is System, Light, or Dark, kept per browser. System is what a browser starts on: it follows your computer's light or dark appearance, and follows it live when it changes. Light and Dark pin one theme. The sidebar's sun and moon switch the same setting: under System they pin the theme opposite the one on screen, and picking System here goes back to following the computer.

Optional features

/console/settings?s=features

Optional features are the parts of Seamless you can switch on and off, and they ship off: a fresh install exposes none of them until you turn one on. The section renders one card per feature - a toggle, an Enabled/Disabled pill, what the feature is, a generated line naming exactly what switching it off hides, and a live count of the data it holds either way ("Data kept: 12 trials across 3 labs").

There are six today:

Research labs & trials owns the Labs and Trials screens, the trials search scope, and the lab_open, trial_record, and trial_query MCP tools. Screens and tools move together on purpose, so an agent never sees a tool for a screen you switched off.

Momentum is gentle progress cues woven into existing screens -- plan finish lines, capture streaks, knowledge payoffs, and project growth -- judged from real activity, never invented. It owns no screens or tools of its own; turning it on adds seven surfaces where you already look:

  • Plan finish-line cards on the Overview attention strip: any plan at least 80% done gets one positive card naming the exact remaining steps ("seambench -- one step from shipped"), linking to the plan, with a thin progress bar drawn to the plan's exact done/total percent. The agent briefing's plan line carries the same emphasis, so agents are nudged to close it too.
  • The capture calendar on Sessions: a year of daily activity, cell intensity from sessions per day, a distinct dot on days that captured knowledge (a session left findings, a memory, a note, or a trial), and two quiet numbers -- the current capture streak and the longest ever. The streak counts covered days, so it rewards capture, not raw usage; a streak of seven covered days or more earns a small flame beside the number, and the number itself stays verbatim. The grid is an instrument, not wallpaper: hovering a cell reads out its day, clicking one focuses the session map on exactly that day (a clearable chip names the focus; picking a time window widens back out), and the grid is keyboard-walkable -- arrows move a day or a week, Enter focuses, all without a page reload.
  • Knowledge payoff moments: the first time a memory is read by a session other than the one that wrote it, the moment lands in the activity ledger ("gotcha chroma-boot-race just paid off for the first time") -- once per memory, ever -- and the Overview rail gains a Memory of the month panel naming the last 30 days' top-utility memory with the counts behind the claim.
  • Maturity stages on the project board and detail header: each project earns a latched stage -- seedling, sprouting, established, deep-rooted -- from real thresholds over age, memories, event volume, and reach. Stages never regress, and the pill's tooltip states exactly what the next stage asks for.
  • The plan-shipped settle on Plans: the task transition that closes a plan's last step -- wherever it lands, an agent shipping over MCP included -- mints a once-ever plan.shipped moment. The plan's row settles with a single wash when it happens while you are watching, the ledger renders it under its own flag icon, and the Plans header counts the local month: "Plans shipped this month: N".
  • Milestone moments in the activity ledger: a short latched set of honest firsts and counts -- a project's 100th/500th/1000th memory, its 1000th answered recall, its first supersession, its first shipped plan, and its birthdays -- each minted once ever and rendered under an award glyph with the exact claim ("100 memories written in seamless"). Milestones accumulate in the ledger only; there is no trophy screen.
  • Witnessed unlocks on Settings: the utility-activation table's armed note upgrades to the date each stage unlocked, so a latch that used to flip silently is witnessed.

Motion keeps one register: every animation plays once -- on a live arrival or on first render -- and nothing loops except the existing pulse idioms. A moment already on screen when the page loads renders plain; only a new arrival over the live feed animates. prefers-reduced-motion stills all of it, and the shipped-plan settle is the ceiling: no confetti and no toasts, which belong to gamification's arcade on Now.

Momentum keeps the console's judged-numbers ethos: every number is real and verifiable, empty states say so honestly, and there are no punishment mechanics -- an inactive day is an empty cell, never a warning, and nothing nags or expires. Off (the default), none of it renders and none of it is computed: no latch moves and no moment is minted. Moments minted while it was on stay in the event history (nothing is ever deleted), though milestone rows leave the activity feeds until it returns.

Gamification is the arcade layer of the Now screen. Where momentum asks "is this knowledge practice building on itself?", gamification plays back "how hard is the fleet running right now?" - and an owner who enjoys one framing may find the other noisy, so they toggle separately. It owns no screens or tools of its own; turning it on adds four surfaces to Now:

  • The day tape: today's judged output - tasks closed, memories and notes written, plans touched, sessions started - each cell against its trailing 7-day daily average.
  • The personal-records rail: latched bests (most tasks closed in a day, most memories written in a day, most agents live at once). Records only ever move forward, like maturity stages; an unset record reads "today could be the day".
  • The hot-streak pulse: the last ten minutes' event count beside the titlebar pulse, catching fire past a fixed floor. The count is shown verbatim either way, so the claim stays verifiable.
  • Celebration moments: a record falling or a plan shipping its last step today renders a moment chip - and when one lands while you are watching, a toast and a brief confetti burst (skipped under reduced motion). A record crossing is minted into the event ledger at most once per record per day.

The same guardrails as momentum apply: every number is judged from recorded activity, never invented, and there are no punishment mechanics - a quiet day is an empty tape, never a warning. Off (the default), none of it is computed, no record latch is written, and the Now page carries zero trace of it.

Write screening is the only feature that changes what agents receive rather than what the console shows. On, every agent write to a memory or note is screened, the suspicious ones - and any change to a binding rule by a session that read outside text, and any supersede or delete of a constraint - wait on the Held screen instead of landing, and briefing and recall lines carry owner-confirmed or agent-written marks. Its card's data line counts the writes waiting; turning it off stops screening new writes and releases none of them. With restricted local accounts configured, the card says the Held screen stays for their proposals and only its screening parts go. The write screening guide has the screens, the reasons and the events.

Repo locks owns the Locks screen, the locks_list, locks_declare, locks_acquire and locks_release MCP tools, and seam lock: locks on a repository's refs that agents declare once and hold while they land changes. Turning it off deletes no lock and no declaration.

Diary owns the Diary screen - a page for each day of work, at every level, the first row of the Work group - and one in-page surface, the Open in Diary link on a Sessions day view. Turn it on here, or with features.diary: true in the config file or SEAMLESS_FEATURES_DIARY=true. Off (the default), there is no sidebar row, palette entry, shortcut, link or script, and /console/diary answers with the switched-off page. It owns no MCP tools. The token record underneath is kept either way: the usage ledger and the event log the Diary reads are written whether it is on or off, so the history is there the moment you turn it on. Turning it on adds one cost that is not presentation: while it is on, a Claude Code prompt keeps its session's usage ledger current, read after the prompt is answered, at most once every three minutes a conversation (mid-session usage). With it off, every hook answers and writes exactly as before.

Nothing is ever deleted. Switching a feature off gates exposure and nothing else: the trials stay in the database, its screens answer with a short "switched off" page that links back here (a JSON caller gets a 403), and switching it back on restores every surface exactly as it was. That is what the data-kept line on each card is for - it reports the feature's own rows whether it is on or off.

When the change lands has four different answers:

Surface When
The console Immediately - nav entries, screens, the search scope, and the overview tiles appear or disappear on the next render.
A tool call Immediately - a disabled feature's tool is refused as an unknown tool, whatever list the caller is holding.
A hook Immediately - the Diary's mid-session usage read follows the switch from the next Claude Code prompt, with no restart.
The agent briefing The next session start - momentum's finish-line emphasis reads the same stored override the console gates on.
A client's tool list The next time it lists tools, in practice its next session. Seamless declares listChanged: false and sends no tool-list notification, so a connected client keeps the list it already has.
The client-side skill The next seamlessd install-hooks run. The daemon does not reach into ~/.claude/skills on a toggle, so seamlessd doctor raises an info line while a skill for a disabled feature is still sitting in a client's skill home.

Saving writes a stored override row in the database - the same layer the briefing form uses. It wins over file and env, never touches your config file, and holds until Reset to file + env clears it; reset means back to the file/env configuration, which unless you set features: there is off.

One override can be in force without you having set it. Upgrading an installation that already holds trial data seeds the override with research on, so a feature that now ships off does not disappear from under data you were already using. That is why the section states that a stored override is in force rather than crediting you with the choice - and reset clears it like any other. At Basic the section keeps the cards, what each hides, and the data-kept line, and leaves out the agent tool names and the precedence line.

Your setup

/console/settings?s=setup

Read-only facts in plain words: the version, the machine the daemon runs on, the config file (with a link that opens it in your editor, or a note that the daemon runs on defaults and environment variables), the data folder, the database file and its size, which agent clients have recorded sessions and when each was last active, whether semantic recall is on - and when it is off, what to do about it - whether the gardener is running and how often, how often backups run, how many are kept and when the last one was made, and links to these docs. No budgets or policy numbers: those live in Knowledge engine.

Updates

/console/settings?s=updates

The automatic update check and automatic updates in plain words: the Mode - whether this install checks for new releases, and whether it installs them by itself or only tells you, and why (a release build checks by default, a build from source does not, and only an install the installer made, or a peer_auth system daemon in the guide's layout, updates itself) - what a check sends (one anonymous request to api.github.com every few hours; nothing when checks are off), the installed version and kind of build, the command that updates this install (with a copy button, labeled To update by hand on an install that updates itself), the newest release with its date and release notes - or "up to date" - and when the daemon last checked and checks next, including a streak of failed checks and why.

The note at the top says who decided the switches: Default for this build, Set in the config file or environment, Set in this console, or Automatic updates set in this console, with Reset to the config file beside a console choice. Turning checks off from here always works for you; an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and a paired device but for your own hands through a relay, may turn checks and automatic updates on, never off. Turning them on does not work when the config file or SEAMLESS_UPDATE_CHECK says false: that is final, the switch shows locked, and the form refuses - false promises no update traffic at all. Check now asks GitHub once, right away (not more than once a minute).

On an install that updates itself, the section adds Automatic updates - on or off, who decided, and Turn automatic updates off / on, which update.auto: false in the config file or environment locks off - and, while they apply, Next update (the release it installs next and what it waits for: the soak, live agent sessions, or a lull after its deadline), Paused, Held back, Skipped releases and Next try. Updating now and Last attempt appear whenever there is one; Last attempt carries the outcome, the updater's own error and its log path - the one place in the console either appears - and, when the updater refused to start, the fix. Update to v0.7.3 now installs the newest release at once after a confirm - skipping the soak, the idle wait, skipped releases and the backoff - and the daemon restarts to finish. Resume automatic updates appears while they are paused or holding releases back.

With update.release_signers set in the config file or environment, an Owner-signed releases row names the file the updater holds every release to, and the last release it refused and why: it carried no owner's signature, was signed by a key the file does not list, or its signature did not verify. Without the key the row is not there. The console can neither set nor clear it.

When a newer release is out, the Home health strip's version fact turns into v0.7.2 -- v0.7.3 available and links here - its hover says whether it installs by itself, and when - and a toast announces it if the console is open when the daemon finds it. While an update runs, the fact reads v0.7.2 -- updating to v0.7.3, and once v0.7.3 is serving and the updater is only confirming it, v0.7.3 -- confirming the update (Updating now says confirming too). The daemon re-reads the updater's record every few seconds while an update runs, so both clear soon after it is confirmed. For a day after the daemon starts on a new version, every page carries a banner - "Seamless updated to v0.7.3 (from v0.7.2)" - with the release notes and Got it, which hides it for that tab. It also says when Codex's hooks changed with the update (re-approve them in Codex's /hooks) or the installer reported warnings (run seamlessd install-hooks). For a week after automatic updates pause themselves, or after an update the daemon started does not apply, every page also carries a warning banner pointing here.

Backups

/console/settings?s=backups

Scheduled backups of the whole instance into one folder you choose, the backups found there, and restore. Backups in the console walks through it; this is what each card holds.

Automatic backups, the status card:

  • whether automatic backups are on, how often they run and how many are kept - or why they are off: turned off here, backup.auto: false in the config file, or a build from source, which backs up only when you turn it on;
  • the newest backup: when, its size, and how many memories and notes in how many projects it holds;
  • when the next backup runs, or Up to date: nothing has changed since the last backup, with when it checks next;
  • a backup under way, while it runs;
  • the automatic runs' failure streak - how many failed in a row, since when, and the last one's reason - with Try again, which runs the schedule's backup now;
  • the folder, with a copy button, and Back up now, which makes a backup marked Made by you whatever the schedule says.

Schedule and folder, the form:

  • Back up automatically. A run is skipped when nothing has changed since the last backup, or when the disk is short of room.
  • How often: Every hour, Every 6 hours, Every day or Every week. An interval set in the config file (anything from 1h to 720h) shows among them as itself.
  • Automatic backups to keep, 1 to 100. Older automatic backups are deleted after the next one. Backups you make yourself and safety backups are never deleted automatically.
  • Folder, with a live check as you type (it only looks, never writes) and chips for the places on this machine this account can write to: iCloud Drive, cloud folders and external disks on macOS, Dropbox and external disks on Linux, OneDrive and other drives on Windows, and Seamless's data folder.

Save stores only what differs from the settings in force; a new folder is created and tested with a write first. Reset to the config file makes the settings follow the config file again. The bar at the top says where the values come from: Default for this build, Following the config file, or Set in this console with the fields you set.

Available backups, the list, newest first: the backups in the chosen folder and in Seamless's data folder (~/.seamless/backups, where the safety and pre-update backups stay). Each row has:

  • when, the kind in words - Automatic, Made by you, Before restore, Before updating from v0.8.1 or Exported - the size, and the machine it came from when another Seamless made it;
  • What it holds: the file's path, and per project the memories, notes, tasks and sessions, beside vs now, how many more or fewer memories and notes the project holds now. A locked project shows its name and the backup's counts, never what it holds now. A project that is no longer here says so, and one that is only here now shows dashes;
  • Restore… and Delete. An iCloud placeholder (download it in Finder first) and a backup a newer Seamless made (update to restore it) cannot be restored and say why.

Restore… opens a confirm card in the backup's row, with a link that works without script:

  • it compares the backup with now (how many more or fewer memories, notes and sessions this install holds);
  • two choices: Replace all data with this backup (your current data is saved as a backup first, so you can undo it) or Only bring back what's missing (nothing you have now changes). A knowledge-only backup offers only the merge;
  • what a restore leaves alone: locks, passkeys, repo routes and console settings stay as they are now, and no project's privacy is loosened;
  • Restore, or Restore with passkey under the peer_auth gate. Without a usable passkey, the card names why and shows the terminal command instead, with a copy button.

Then a progress card lists the steps: Checking the backup, Preparing the restored data (replace) or Saving your current data (merge), Restarting Seamless, Done, and for a replace, Saving your previous data as a backup. The page waits through the restart and draws the section again in place. Cancel restore is offered while a restore is staged. On Windows, the card names seamlessd restart, to run within an hour, after which a staged restore is dropped.

After the restart, the result card says what was restored, where the previous data was saved, and anything the restore kept of today (a stricter privacy setting, locked projects the backup did not have), with Undo this restore - the confirm card for the safety backup - and Dismiss. A restore that did not finish, expired or stopped partway says so there instead.

Elsewhere:

  • Settings > Your setup has a Backups row: how often, how many are kept, and the last backup.
  • Every page carries an alert while automatic backups are in trouble, linking here. Automatic backups are failing. appears when two automatic runs in a row did not finish, with the first failure's time and the reason. Automatic backups are overdue. appears when none has finished for three intervals. Got it hides it for that tab until a new episode begins.
  • System draws backups as a core part, on, off, failing or overdue.

Briefing

/console/settings?s=briefing

What every new agent session starts with. Three presets lead the section - Lean (a short briefing: the binding rules, the freshest memories, little else), Balanced (exactly the defaults), and Rich (more rules in full, more recent work, and family memories) - each card showing the numbers that set it apart. Picking one fills the form; nothing is saved until you save. Below them, Customize holds every knob, grouped by what it shapes - the memory index, recent work, the planning horizon, the project family, utility ranking, and the safety ceiling - with each knob's "0 means" note under it. Customize is open by default at Advanced. The section marks the preset your saved values equal, or Custom when they match none, and re-marks it as you edit.

Saving writes a runtime override row in the DB. It layers over the file/env values and wins until reset, and it applies from the next session start - no daemon restart. It never touches your config file, so seamless.yaml stays the thing you wrote. The token budget (budgets.max_briefing_tokens) is not a briefing knob and no preset moves it. The form validates: a non-numeric knob or a value that fails Briefing.Validate() comes back as an error flash, not a silently-dropped save.

The preview shows the <seam-briefing> a new session in one project would start with, under the values the form holds right now, saved or not. It sits between the presets and Customize, or beside the form when the section is wide enough. Pick a preset or change a knob and it follows within a moment. It also shows the token estimate against budgets.max_briefing_tokens and the hard cap, and flags a briefing that runs over the budget (only constraints, pinned stages, and starred rows can put it there) or would be cut at the cap. The project picker lists the registered projects and opens on the one your agents worked in last. A preview is a read: it saves nothing, records no event, and no agent receives it, so it never counts toward retrieval stats or utility. Values the save would refuse, it refuses with the same message. For scripts, GET /console/settings/briefing/preview?project=<slug>&format=json previews the saved values. POST to the same path, with the form's fields plus project, previews unsaved ones. It is the one POST in the console that writes nothing, which is why it is not in the table of write routes above.

The utility ranking group holds utility_weight (utility's share of the briefing sort key; 0 restores pure recency) and utility_mode (auto arms each project as its demand history matures, on everywhere now, off never). Where each scope stands against the readiness gates is in Knowledge engine. See Sessions & briefings for how the blended order behaves once active.

Workspaces

/console/settings?s=workspaces

How repositories resolve to project scopes, and which projects share context. Project families are editable here: create, rename, edit, or delete the named groupings that seamlessd family manages from the CLI - the same project_families setting, so a change on either surface shows up on the other. Members are chosen from a closed picker of registered projects; the CLI is the route for pre-registering a slug that does not exist yet. Below it, one bounded directory lists every scope with its repo routes and family tags. At Advanced each route also names the machine it lives on, and repo paths that resolve to no project are listed as unbound.

Knowledge engine

/console/settings?s=engine

The machinery, in three groups.

Recall - the embedder card shows the active provider and model, and when embeddings are off, the exact cause, with distinct copy for the owner off switch, the no-key lexical fallback, and a config error. The off/auto switch is a settings row read once at serve start, so the page flags a pending restart whenever the stored switch disagrees with the running process. Beside it, the stored-vector counts: totals, the not-yet-embedded backlog, and a per-model table that badges models the running embedder no longer writes as stale - re-embed everything rewrites the corpus with the active model in the background.

Ranking - the utility activation by scope table lists every scope with each readiness gate against its threshold (demand events, memories touched, history age - met gates turn green) and, for scopes still building, spells out exactly what remains before auto arms ("needs 7 more events, 3d more history"). A per-scope force overrides the latch in either direction; when the global mode is on or off, the table says the per-scope state is dormant until auto returns.

Storage & policy - read-only: the data folder, the context budgets, the database (path, size on disk including the WAL, schema version), and the gardener's cadence and policy. Change these through the config file or environment, then restart.

See Configuration for what each knob does, and Sessions & briefings for what they tune.

Event detail

/console/events/{id}

What a Recent-activity or timeline row links to: a compact event review workspace with the event's agent/session attribution, verbatim injected or transport content, surfaced memories resolved to their live index entries (or flagged missing), remaining payload fields, and raw JSON (the last two at the Advanced level; ?format=json always carries them). The Interactions inspector uses the same content model in a side pane; opening the full page adds context without changing the underlying event.

Errors

A bad or stale URL renders a styled, layout-wrapped error page with a way back, rather than dropping you on a bare 404 page not found -- including any /console/ path no route claims, which gets a search box and links to the common destinations. A 404 names the missing entity and a 400 names the bad parameter and its valid values. A 500 stays generic in the browser - the detail is in the log, not the response. Fragment fetches (?peek=1) get a fragment-shaped error, since a full page injected into the detail pane would nest the whole console inside itself.
